**Environmental-Tracer Residence Time, Graph Topology and Inverse Hydrogeochemistry in Data-Limited Aquifers: A Critical Review**

Dickson Abdul-Wahab, Dickson Adomako, Gibrilla Abass, Ebenezer Aquisman Asare, Samuel Ganyaglo,  

**Abstract**

Groundwater assessment in data-limited aquifers remains constrained by non-unique interpretations of residence time, hydraulic connectivity and hydrogeochemical evolution because tracer-based ages, graph-based connectivity and inverse reaction models are commonly applied separately. This critical review evaluates isotope and environmental-tracer residence-time methods, graph-topological representations of aquifer connectivity, and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling as complementary tools for reducing interpretive ambiguity in sparse-data settings. Literature was identified through searches in Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar and Consensus, supported by hand-searching of key reviews and screening of public benchmark resources, including USGS and IAEA datasets. The review corpus was selective rather than exhaustive and was assessed using five criteria: data requirements, assumptions, uncertainty, applicability to data-limited settings and integration potential. The review shows that multi-tracer strategies are essential but rarely available in data-limited regions; graph topology can formalise directed, confidence-weighted hydraulic connections but must be distinguished from statistical and reaction graphs; and PHREEQC/NETPATH inverse modelling is weakened by subjective flow-path selection and incomplete reporting of viable solutions. The synthesis proposes staged workflows in which residence-time classes constrain graph edges, graph topology guides inverse model pair selection, and reaction models are filtered by age, mineralogy and saturation-index evidence. Because the framework is conceptual and has not yet been tested on a field dataset, it should be regarded as a basis for future software implementation, benchmark testing and field validation rather than as a fully validated operational tool.

**Keywords: Environmental tracers, Groundwater age uncertainty, Lumped parameter models,   Flow-path connectivity, PHREEQC/NETPATH modelling**

**1\. Introduction**

Groundwater residence time can be broadly defined as the elapsed time a water parcel spends within the saturated zone between its point of recharge entry and its eventual exit at a well, spring, stream, or model boundary, is a foundational quantity in hydrogeological assessment (Hssaisoune et al., 2022; Newman et al., 2021; Mudimbu et al., 2024). In the reservoir-theoretic formulation, the mean residence time of discharge at steady state is equivalent to the ratio of total aquifer water volume to the recharge inflow rate, which in practice translates to porosity multiplied by saturated thickness divided by recharge (Newman et al., 2021). More completely, residence time is characterised by residence time distributions (RTDs), which describe the full range of times water parcels spend traversing the flow domain from recharge to discharge and are fundamental to linking tracer observations to physical aquifer structure (Hssaisoune et al., 2022). It is important to distinguish residence time from related but conceptually distinct temporal quantities: recharge timing refers to when and where infiltration enters the system rather than to its subsequent subsurface duration; advective travel time describes particle motion along a specific flow path; and aquifer hydraulic response time characterises the speed at which heads and storage adjust to external stresses, a quantity governed by transmissivity, storativity, and boundary conditions rather than by tracer-based water age (Vitvar et al., 2022; Allen & Boutt, 2021; Newman et al., 2021).

Groundwater residence time occupies a central role in aquifer assessment for several interconnected reasons. Age tracers distinguish recently recharged modern water from ancient or fossil groundwater, enabling delineation of flow system stratification, inference of recharge rates, and characterisation of confined versus unconfined conditions and multilayer connectivity (Coulidiati et al., 2025; Gilmore et al., 2021). Dynamic vulnerability assessments increasingly integrate RTD models to link temporal changes in groundwater quality with spatial vulnerability maps, using equivalent residence time along flow nets (Banerjee et al., 2023). In managed aquifer recharge, spatially variable transit times govern chemical and pathogen attenuation along flow paths, directly controlling risk to downstream users (Scanlon et al., 2023). Residence time is equally central to water-resource sustainability analyses, where distinguishing actively recharged water from non-renewable fossil reserves depends on reliable age inference, a critical distinction given that a vast majority of the world's groundwater is fossil yet remains susceptible to modern contamination (Jasechko et al., 2017; Cuthbert et al., 2023). Despite its acknowledged importance, estimating groundwater residence time in complex or poorly monitored systems remains a persistent methodological challenge, particularly in semi-arid and data-limited regions where episodic recharge, sparse monitoring networks, and strong subsurface heterogeneity combine to produce highly uncertain and often non-unique age estimates (Borzí, 2025; Van Wyk et al., 2024; Beyene et al., 2023). This temporal uncertainty is only one part of the interpretive problem.

Nuclear and environmental isotope tracers provide temporal and source-specific information that conventional hydrochemical indicators alone cannot supply. The principal tracers span a hierarchy of residence-time windows. Tritium (3H), with a half-life of 12.43 years, identifies post-1950 modern recharge over timescales of years to a few decades, and its absence implies residence times exceeding approximately 50 years or significant confinement (Gilmore et al., 2021; Etuk et al., 2025; Coulidiati et al., 2025). The combined 3H/3He method, exploiting the ingrowth of tritiogenic 3He from 3H decay within a system closed to helium loss after recharge, extends robust apparent-age estimation to approximately 60 years in shallow, predominantly unconfined aquifers (Gilmore et al., 2021). Carbon-14, with a half-life of 5,730 years, is the principal tool for constraining residence times of hundreds to approximately 40,000 years in confined and deep sedimentary aquifers, though geochemical corrections for dead-carbon contributions from aquifer mineral dissolution remain a critical interpretive challenge (Coulidiati et al., 2025; Martínez et al., 2025). For very old groundwaters, chlorine-36 (36Cl) and krypton-81 (81Kr) extend age resolution to 104–106 years in deep confined systems (Martínez et al., 2025; Schubert et al., 2024). Complementary tools include short-lived radionuclides such as radon-222 (222Rn) and sulphur-35 (35S) for very short residence times of hours to months in highly dynamic or shallow systems, and helium-4 (4He) accumulation for extremely old deep waters, often combined with noble-gas recharge temperatures to provide corrections for excess terrigenic helium in fractured or basaltic aquifers (Gilmore et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022; Schubert et al., 2024). The comparative dating ranges of these tracers are illustrated in Figure 2\. While isotope tracers offer clear advantages over conventional hydrochemistry for age determination and recharge source identification, their application requires specialised laboratory infrastructure, strict sampling protocols, and careful treatment of mixing, geochemical alteration, and non-unique input functions, constraints that are especially limiting in resource-constrained and data-scarce settings (Sankoh et al., 2021; Banerjee et al., 2023).

An aquifer is appropriately characterised as data-limited when the information necessary for hydrogeological characterisation, monitoring, and modelling is systematically sparse, short, or spatially uneven. The operational consequences are wide-ranging. In terms of monitoring infrastructure, data-limited settings typically feature few piezometers with discontinuous water-level records, absent or incomplete pumping test databases, coarse regional geological maps that leave aquifer boundaries and internal stratigraphy poorly defined, and boundary conditions that cannot be reliably specified (Borzí, 2025; Coulidiati et al., 2025; El-Agha et al., 2023). At the hydrochemical level, studies from East Africa demonstrate that groundwater chemistry surveys concentrate near known problem areas and urban centres, with approximately 71% of samples collected only once at each monitoring point, rendering seasonal variability and trend analyses largely unresolvable (Nowicki et al., 2023). This pattern of one-off, spatially clustered sampling makes it fundamentally difficult to distinguish real spatial heterogeneity from sampling artefacts and to reconstruct geochemical evolution along flow paths. The review is global in methodological scope but uses semi-arid and African data-limited aquifers as a recurring transferability lens. This framing is deliberate: many tracer, graph and inverse-modelling methods have been developed or benchmarked using well-instrumented aquifers and public datasets from North America, Europe and Asia, whereas their intended application in many African semi-arid settings must contend with sparse monitoring networks, incomplete borehole and pumping-test metadata, limited access to specialised isotope analysis, strong lithological heterogeneity and episodic recharge (Borzí, 2025; Nowicki et al., 2023; Beyene et al., 2023; Van Wyk et al., 2024; Mudimbu et al., 2024; Ferrer et al., 2019).

Several categories of missing data exert disproportionate influence on interpretation. Absence of environmental isotope data, particularly 3H, 14C, and stable water isotopes, prevents direct constraints on residence time and recharge source, leaving flow paths and water age as essentially hypothetical (Nowicki et al., 2023; Coulidiati et al., 2025). Incomplete recharge histories, combined with strong spatial heterogeneity in lithology, fracture density, and vadose zone thickness, characteristics typical of semi-arid basement and sedimentary aquifers across sub-Saharan Africa, generate recharge estimates that can differ by orders of magnitude between methods, producing inferred residence times and water balances that must be treated as highly approximate (Beyene et al., 2023; Borzí, 2025; Van Wyk et al., 2024). The coexistence of these deficiencies means that flow paths, apparent ages, and geochemical interpretations remain highly non-unique, dependent on the conceptual model chosen, and poorly amenable to independent validation (Borzí, 2025; Motalib, 2025; Ntona et al., 2022).

A fundamental problem in applied hydrogeochemistry is that groundwater residence time, while indicative of the duration of water–rock contact, is insufficient on its own to explain observed groundwater chemistry. Lithology, mineralogy, redox state, pH, ionic strength, and the geometry of mixing zones all exert independent control on solute concentrations and isotopic activities, such that groundwaters of comparable residence time can exhibit radically different chemistries, and waters of similar composition may reflect entirely different flow histories (Vengosh et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2024; Wali et al., 2024). In semi-arid basement aquifers, major-ion chemistry is primarily controlled by silicate weathering and specific mineral equilibria rather than by age patterns alone (Coulidiati et al., 2025), while geogenic contaminants including arsenic, fluoride, selenium, and uranium are mobilised by combinations of basin geology, tectonics, and local redox conditions that operate largely independently of residence time (Cao et al., 2024). Hydrological and mixing dynamics introduce further complexity: in groundwater–surface water exchange zones, changing flow paths, mixing ratios, and hyporheic exchange create strong spatial redox and nutrient gradients driven by hydrological state transitions rather than by water age alone (Gómez‐Gener et al., 2021; Banerjee & Ganguly, 2023). 

A second source of ambiguity is spatial: sparse data often leave the connectivity among wells, recharge zones and discharge points unresolved. Graph topology offers a structurally explicit approach to representing these complexities. By treating wells, springs, and landscape recharge nodes as vertices and plausible hydraulic connections as directed edges, graph-based frameworks formalise hypothesised flow connections, organise recharge–discharge pathways as directed networks, and clarify spatial relationships among monitoring points within the overall connectivity structure, capabilities that conventional piezometric maps and purely statistical hydrochemical analyses do not routinely provide (Dwivedi et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024; Borzí, 2025). Graph topology metrics, including path length, connectivity centrality, and community structure, can highlight critical hydraulic links, potential barriers to flow, and aquifer sub-domains in ways that substitute or complement full numerical hydraulic models when detailed parameterisation is infeasible (Yu et al., 2024).

A third ambiguity is geochemical: even when water chemistry is measured, multiple reaction pathways can explain the same observed composition. Inverse hydrogeochemical modelling provides a third, reaction-diagnostic dimension by reconstructing the mineral dissolution, ion exchange, and mixing processes that account for observed chemistry differences along prescribed flow paths (Tziritis et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2025; Masoud et al., 2025). However, these three methodological strands are consistently treated in parallel rather than in concert in the existing literature: isotope and tracer reviews are typically paired with flow models and budgets but not with graph connectivity; inverse geochemical models are applied along assumed flow paths without independent topological constraint; and network-based representations of aquifer systems, where they appear, seldom incorporate age or reaction information (Borzí, 2025; Banerjee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021). The conceptual relationship between these three domains is summarised in Figure 1\. Reducing non-uniqueness and improving aquifer-process interpretation in data-limited settings requires an integrated framework that employs isotope-derived age constraints, topology-informed flow connectivity, and reaction-based geochemical fitting in a mutually constraining workflow (Borzí, 2025; Ali et al., 2024; Medici & Langman, 2022).

Several major scientific questions at the intersection of these three domains remain unresolved. These include: how residence time distributions and mixing structures can be encoded in graph topology to constrain inverse reaction models; how connectivity, residence time, and reaction pathways can be jointly inferred under conditions of data scarcity; and how uncertainty should be propagated and communicated across an integrated framework of this kind (Starn et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2025; Borzí, 2025; Tziritis et al., 2023). Few reviews identified in the searched literature explicitly integrate isotope-based residence time, graph-based groundwater connectivity and inverse hydrogeochemistry within a single operational framework for data-limited aquifer systems. Existing reviews call for integration of diverse data sources and models, but the practical coupling of age constraints, directed connectivity and edge-based reaction modelling remains underdeveloped (Borzí, 2025; Banerjee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021).

The present article addresses this gap through a critical review with the following objectives: (i) to evaluate the current state of environmental-tracer residence-time methods with explicit attention to uncertainty and mixed-age groundwater; (ii) to assess graph-topology approaches as tools for representing groundwater connectivity in sparse-data environments; (iii) to critique inverse hydrogeochemical modelling methods with respect to non-uniqueness and flow-path dependence; and (iv) to propose integrated workflows, evaluation metrics, and a research agenda for data-limited aquifer characterisation. The review draws primarily on peer-reviewed literature and publicly available benchmark datasets to improve the traceability and transferability of the proposed framework. Conference abstracts, preprints or technical resources were retained only where they clarified methodological development, regional context or data availability, and they were not used as sole support for major conclusions. Because this is a critical review rather than a systematic review, the literature corpus was selected to support methodological comparison and conceptual synthesis rather than exhaustive retrieval. To improve transparency, the methods section reports the databases searched, search-term clusters, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the analytical criteria used to compare studies. Table 1 summarises the principal nuclear and environmental tracers discussed in Section 3, and Table 3 provides a comparison of graph-topology approaches reviewed in Section 4\.

**2\. Methods**

**2.1 Review Design and Scope**

This article is structured as a critical review rather than a systematic or scoping review. A critical review differs from a systematic review in that it does not aspire to exhaustive identification of every eligible study; instead, it evaluates methodological quality, theoretical coherence, and the degree to which reported findings resolve or fail to resolve the specific research questions (Borzí, 2025). This design is appropriate here because the three bodies of literature being synthesised that is, environmental-tracer residence-time estimation, graph topology in groundwater systems, and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling, are methodologically heterogeneous, draw on different disciplinary conventions, and have not previously been evaluated under a unified interpretive framework. The review scope is therefore defined by its central intellectual objective: to determine whether, and under what conditions, integrating these three methodological traditions reduces the non-uniqueness and interpretive ambiguity that characterises groundwater assessment in data-limited aquifers (Banerjee et al., 2023; Borzí, 2025). The review does not seek a comprehensive inventory of all studies using any of the three methods; rather, it critically evaluates representative, high-quality studies that illuminate key method strengths, failure modes, and cross-method integration opportunities. The scope is bounded in time to peer-reviewed literature published predominantly from 2015 onwards, with older foundational studies included where they establish methodological principles that remain authoritative (Han & Plummer, 2015; Cartwright et al., 2017, 2019).

**2.2 Literature-Search Strategy and Databases**

Literature searches were conducted across Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar and the Consensus AI-powered academic search engine. Consensus was used as a supplementary semantic-search tool rather than as a replacement for conventional bibliographic databases. Records identified through Consensus were retained only where they could be verified through publisher metadata, DOI records, Scopus, Web of Science or Google Scholar. This verification step was used to reduce the risk that AI-mediated search would alter the evidence base through incomplete, irrelevant or unverifiable retrieval. Searches were organised around three thematic clusters: residence-time and isotope-dating methods; graph topology and groundwater connectivity; and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling. The search strategy was designed to identify representative methodological studies, recent applications and key reviews rather than to produce an exhaustive PRISMA-style corpus. Because the article is a critical review, records were selected for methodological relevance, quality of evidence, uncertainty treatment and transferability to data-limited aquifer settings. Searches used Boolean combinations of terms drawn from three thematic clusters: (i) residence time and isotope dating, including search strings such as "groundwater residence time," "groundwater age tracer," "tritium dating," "radiocarbon groundwater," "3H/3He," "CFCs groundwater," "lumped parameter model," and "transit time distribution"; (ii) graph topology and connectivity, including "graph theory groundwater," "network topology aquifer," "MODPATH particle tracking," "directed graph hydrology," "preferential flow network," and "groundwater connectivity graph"; and (iii) inverse hydrogeochemical modelling, including "PHREEQC inverse modelling," "NETPATH mass balance," "saturation index groundwater," "inverse geochemistry data-limited," and "reaction pathway groundwater." Additional searches combined these clusters to retrieve studies addressing more than one methodological strand simultaneously. Reference lists of key reviews were hand-searched to identify older foundational studies not returned in database queries. The IAEA Hydrology Section and USGS National Water Information System were searched for publicly accessible isotope and tracer datasets applicable to method validation. The search strategy is summarised in Supplementary Table S1. The table records the databases and repositories searched, thematic query clusters, representative Boolean strings, screening logic and the role of each search component in the review. Because this article is a critical review rather than a systematic review, the table is intended to improve transparency of the evidence-identification process rather than to provide a PRISMA-style account of exhaustive retrieval, deduplication and screening counts.

**2.3 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria**

Studies were included if they reported primary empirical or modelling results directly addressing at least one of the three core topics, namely environmental-tracer groundwater residence-time estimation, graph-based representations of aquifer connectivity, or inverse hydrogeochemical modelling. Studies combining two or more of these methods were given particular priority. The review also included studies demonstrating specific method limitations, bias sources, or failure modes, because critical evaluation of weakness is as central to the review objective as identification of strength. Studies were included regardless of whether they explicitly addressed data-limited aquifer settings, provided that their methodological insights were transferable to such settings with appropriate modification. Studies meeting the topical inclusion criteria were prioritised according to methodological relevance and evidence quality. Priority was given to studies that reported sufficient hydrogeological context, clearly described tracer or modelling assumptions, included uncertainty or sensitivity analysis, used multiple lines of evidence, provided field or model validation, and reported enough data to permit methodological interpretation. For isotope studies, tracer-suite adequacy and correction procedures were emphasised; for graph studies, the physical basis for node definition, edge direction and edge weighting was emphasised; and for inverse hydrogeochemical studies, phase-list justification, saturation-index screening and reporting of alternative viable solutions were emphasised. Public benchmark datasets were screened separately from literature sources. Dataset inclusion required documented access, relevance to at least one component of the proposed framework, spatial metadata, hydrochemical or isotope variables, and sufficient documentation to evaluate potential use in workflow development or validation. Datasets were not treated as empirical studies unless accompanied by peer-reviewed analysis; rather, they were evaluated as potential resources for testing residence-time inference, graph construction, inverse geochemical modelling or uncertainty propagation.

Exclusion criteria eliminated studies that were purely descriptive field characterisations with no methodological content, duplicate publications from the same study site reporting the same results, grey literature without peer review, and studies focused exclusively on surface-water or vadose-zone hydrology without groundwater tracer application. Studies addressing engineered or industrial settings, such as nuclear waste repositories or geothermal systems, were retained only where their tracer or graph-modelling findings had clear applicability to natural aquifer settings. Studies addressing water distribution networks were included for their graph-topology insights but evaluated with awareness that hydraulically pressurised pipe systems differ fundamentally from porous or fractured aquifer systems (Yu et al., 2024).

**2.4 Analytical Framework for Comparing Methods**

Each methodological domain was evaluated using a consistent set of criteria: data requirements; key assumptions and their hydrogeological preconditions; principal sources of uncertainty and non-uniqueness; applicability to data-limited settings; and evidence of integration with complementary methods. This five-criterion framework was designed to make comparisons interpretable across the isotope, graph-topology, and inverse geochemistry literatures, which differ substantially in terminology, model complexity, and disciplinary norms. Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and Table 4 operationalise these criteria for tracers, age-modelling approaches, graph-topology methods, and inverse hydrogeochemical tools, respectively. A central evaluative question was whether each method's uncertainty can be reduced when the other two methods are used as independent constraints. For isotope methods, the relevant question is whether graph-inferred flow paths and reaction models make tracer ages more interpretable and less equifinal. For graph methods, the question is whether isotope ages and reaction stoichiometry help validate, weight, or reject candidate edges. For inverse geochemical methods, the question is whether topology-constrained flow paths and age-derived reaction-time windows reduce the number of equally plausible reaction solutions (Tziritis et al., 2023; Starn et al., 2021; Borzí, 2025). To distinguish method exposition from evidence synthesis, the central studies used in the critical review were organised by methodological domain, aquifer type, geographic setting, data used, uncertainty treatment, validation approach and relevance to data-limited aquifers. This evidence-matrix logic was used to compare how isotope residence-time methods, graph-topological approaches and inverse hydrogeochemical models perform under different data conditions. The central evidence base used for the critical synthesis is summarised in Supplementary Table S2. The table is not intended as a PRISMA-style exhaustive corpus; rather, it identifies the studies most important to the review’s methodological comparison across isotope residence-time estimation, graph-topological connectivity, inverse hydrogeochemistry, public benchmark datasets and data-limited aquifer transferability.

**2.5 Limits of the Review and Terminology Standardisation**

This review has several acknowledged limitations. First, it does not address in detail the computational implementation of the proposed integrated workflows, which will require dedicated future empirical studies. Second, the literature on graph topology in groundwater is heterogeneous: some studies use graph theory in its strict mathematical sense (Karra et al., 2017; Fandel et al., 2022), while others use the term informally to mean spatial network diagrams derived from field data (Schiavo et al., 2022). This heterogeneity makes cross-study comparison non-trivial. Third, the inverse hydrogeochemical literature uses "flow path" in ways that range from a hydraulically simulated particle track to an assumed spatial sequence of two water samples with no flow-modelling basis (Gastmans et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2020). Such definitional inconsistency directly affects the comparability of non-uniqueness and uncertainty estimates across studies. This critical review is also subject to selection bias because it prioritises studies that illuminate methodological strengths, limitations and integration potential rather than exhaustively cataloguing all applications. English-language and database-indexing bias may have reduced retrieval of regional groundwater studies, particularly from data-limited countries. No formal risk-of-bias scoring was applied; instead, evidence quality was assessed narratively through data completeness, uncertainty treatment, validation, methodological transparency and transferability to data-limited aquifer settings.

To standardise terminology, the following definitions are used consistently throughout this article. "Groundwater age" refers to the elapsed time between recharge and sampling at any point in the flow system. "Apparent age" refers to the tracer-derived estimate of that elapsed time under a specific lumped-parameter model, and is explicitly an approximation. "Mean residence time" refers to the flow-system average of groundwater age at a sampling outlet, as estimated by RTD modelling. "Graph edge" denotes a directed connection between two nodes representing either observed or inferred hydraulic connectivity with an associated confidence weight. "Inverse model" denotes a mass-balance calculation that reconstructs reaction and mixing terms from observed initial and final water chemistry. "Data-limited aquifer" denotes a system where sparse spatial coverage, short temporal records, incomplete tracer suites, or uncharacterised hydrogeological structure prevent reliable independent validation of any single-method interpretation (Borzí, 2025; Nowicki et al., 2023).

**3\. Environmental-Tracer Residence-Time Methods**

**3.1 Conceptual Distinction Between Groundwater Age, Apparent Age and Residence Time**

The conceptual vocabulary of groundwater timing is not yet standardised across hydrogeological practice. At its most general, "groundwater age" denotes the elapsed time since a water parcel recharged the saturated zone and thus represents the true physical travel time from recharge entry to the sampling point (Gilmore et al., 2021; Martínez et al., 2025). When this age is derived from a single isotope tracer under an idealised flow assumption, most commonly the piston-flow model, the result is more precisely called an "apparent age" or "tracer age," because it conflates the true physical age with the simplifying assumptions embedded in the model (Gilmore et al., 2021). The distinction matters enormously in practice: in heterogeneous or mixed aquifers, an apparent age from 3H/3He may differ from a 14C-based apparent age for the same sample, and both may differ from the physically true residence time because mixing, dispersion, and geochemical alteration each affect the tracer signal in tracer-specific ways (Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022; Martínez et al., 2025).

Mean residence time (MRT) elevates analysis from a single sample to the flow-system level: it is the flow-averaged age of all water contributing to a discharge point, well, or spring, and is typically inferred from lumped-parameter models (LPMs) rather than from direct tracer decay equations (Benettin et al., 2022). The full transit-time distribution (TTD) extends this further by describing the probability density of all ages present in the discharge, thereby encoding information about aquifer heterogeneity, mixing, and the relative contributions of young versus old groundwater (Benettin et al., 2022; Gilmore et al., 2021). Most regional groundwater age studies continue to report only apparent piston-flow ages; the explicit estimation of MRT and TTD remains far less common, particularly in data-limited settings where the multi-tracer datasets required for RTD estimation are rarely available (Martínez et al., 2025). This distinction between conceptual, apparent, and distribution-based age is carried consistently throughout Sections 3.2–3.6.

**3.2 Tritium and Tritium-Helium Dating for Young Groundwater**

Tritium (3H) is a radioactive hydrogen isotope naturally produced by cosmic-ray spallation and introduced into the hydrological cycle as tritiated water (HTO). Its half-life of 12.32 years means that detectable 3H (typically greater than approximately 1 tritium unit) in a groundwater sample demonstrates recharge within roughly the last 60 to 70 years; complete absence of 3H implies either confinement, very long residence time, or recharge prior to the atmospheric weapon-test pulse of the 1950s and 1960s (Gilmore et al., 2021; Schubert et al., 2024; Coulidiati et al., 2025). Used alone, 3H provides a binary classification of modern versus pre-modern recharge rather than a precise age, because the declining post-bomb 3H signal makes residence-time calculations without the daughter product ambiguous (Gilmore et al., 2021; Van Rooyen et al., 2020).

The 3H/3He method resolves this limitation by exploiting the ingrowth of tritiogenic 3He (3Hetrit) from 3H decay in a system isolated from helium exchange after recharge. The apparent age is calculated from the ratio of 3Hetrit to remaining 3H using the known decay constant, and crucially does not require reconstruction of the historical atmospheric 3H input record (Gilmore et al., 2021). Isolating 3Hetrit from total measured 3He demands several correction steps: atmospheric helium components (equilibrium solubility and excess air) are computed using multi-noble-gas thermometry from measured Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe concentrations; terrigenic helium from radiogenic and nucleogenic crustal or mantle sources is estimated using the measured 4He excess and an assumed or measured 3He/4He ratio for those sources; and degassing corrections are applied where ΔNe values indicate gas loss (Gilmore et al., 2021). The method is most reliable in shallow, unconfined aquifers with minimal terrigenic 4He inputs, moderate excess air, and negligible degassing; errors in the terrigenic helium correction propagate directly into apparent ages when crustal 4He flux is large (Gilmore et al., 2021). Field applications demonstrate the method's power in contaminated aquifers, for instance, delineating trichloroethylene plume travel times in Quebec, characterising coastal plain recharge in New Jersey, and distinguishing depth-stratified recharge in semi-arid India. While also illustrating that long-screened wells, mixing, and borehole construction can severely limit depth-resolved interpretation (Gilmore et al., 2021; Keesari et al., 2021; Cartwright et al., 2017).

**3.3 Carbon-14 and Correction Problems in Old Groundwater**

Carbon-14 (14C) is the principal dating tool for groundwater with residence times from a few hundred to approximately 40,000 years, with a practical upper limit of about 25,000–30,000 years in most natural settings because of the low 14C activity and associated measurement uncertainties at old ages (Cartwright et al., 2019). The method measures 14C activity in dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), which enters the groundwater system from soil CO2 at recharge, and then applies the radioactive decay law using a reconstructed initial 14C activity (14C₀) to yield a conventional radiocarbon age (Cartwright et al., 2019; Han & Plummer, 2015). The fundamental challenge is that 14C₀ is not directly observable: it must be estimated by correcting for all geochemical processes between recharge and sampling that add 14C-free or isotopically modified carbon to the DIC pool.

The principal 14C correction problem arises from closed-system dissolution of carbonate minerals, which are usually 14C-dead on the timescale of most groundwater systems. This process dilutes 14C in DIC and causes apparent ages to be overestimated if uncorrected (Cartwright et al., 2019; Han & Plummer, 2015). Additional complications include open-system calcite dissolution in the unsaturated zone, which can raise or lower DIC 14C depending on the balance of atmospheric CO2 exchange and mineral dissolution; geogenic CO2 from mantle or metamorphic sources with very low 14C; methanogenesis and oxidation of old organic carbon, each of which add isotopically distinct carbon to the DIC pool; and, in agricultural settings, amendment of soils with anthropogenic carbonate that introduces modern or depleted carbon with site-specific isotopic signatures (Cartwright et al., 2019; Han & Plummer, 2015; Seltzer et al., 2021). Recent applications increasingly pair 14C with dissolved noble gases to more reliably resolve these complex anthropogenic and geochemical dilution effects (Seltzer et al., 2023). Single-sample correction models, including the Pearson, Han–Plummer, IAEA, and Oeschger models, estimate 14C₀ from measured DIC and δ13C using simplified carbonate-chemistry assumptions, but can shift apparent ages by many thousands of years depending on which model is chosen (Han & Plummer, 2015). The statistical 14C–δ13C approach, which fits the curved relationship between these variables across many samples in the same aquifer to infer a system-wide 14C₀, performs better where single-sample models diverge and is particularly suited to semi-arid, geochemically complex confined aquifers (Han & Plummer, 2015; Cartwright et al., 2019). Full geochemical mass-balance models using PHREEQC or NETPATH offer the most rigorous approach in principle, but require extensive mineralogical, isotopic, and chemical data that are typically unavailable in data-limited settings. As summarised in Table 2, all three correction approaches must be considered alongside explicit uncertainty quantification, because 14C ages without stated correction method and uncertainty range carry limited interpretive value.

**3.4 Krypton-85, Chlorine-36, Helium-4, SF6 and CFCs as Complementary Tracers**

The environmental-tracer and anthropogenic-gas tracer toolbox provides complementary windows into residence time that together span from years to millions of years, as illustrated in Figure 2\. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFC-11, CFC-12, CFC-113) and sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) are atmospheric trace gases whose concentrations in recharge water tracked their historically reconstructed atmospheric curves, enabling apparent ages for young groundwater of approximately 0 to 60 years to be computed (Cartwright et al., 2017; Bartyzel & Różański, 2016). Krypton-85 (85Kr), a radioactive noble gas with a half-life of 10.76 years released from nuclear fuel processing, extends young-water dating to similar timescales while avoiding the contamination and terrigenic enrichment problems that affect SF6 in some lithologies (Kagabu et al., 2017; Meyzonnat et al., 2023). In Kumamoto, Japan, 85Kr yielded interpretable ages where CFC and SF6 signals were degraded by artificial additions, demonstrating its particular utility in urban or geologically enriched settings (Kagabu et al., 2017).

Chlorine-36 (36Cl) exploits both the bomb-pulse produced in the 1950s and 1960s, which dates young water similarly to 3H, and its radioactive decay with a half-life of approximately 301,000 years to date very old waters in the range of 104 to 106 years (Purtschert et al., 2022; Martínez et al., 2025). Along a flow path in the Great Artesian Basin, 36Cl and 81Kr provided complementary old-water constraints, with 81Kr anchoring the timescale and allowing recalibration of 36Cl initial ratios that had previously been assumed rather than independently verified (Purtschert et al., 2022; Matsumoto et al., 2020). Helium-4 (4He) accumulates from radiogenic production in crustal minerals along the flow path, and can act as a long-term chronometer for very old groundwater where the local 4He accumulation rate is constrained by geology, though uncertainty in that rate commonly limits 4He to a semi-quantitative old-water indicator (Kazahaya et al., 2007; Broers et al., 2021). The key limitation common to all gas tracers namely, CFC degradation under reducing conditions, terrigenic SF6 enrichment, 36Cl initial ratio assumptions, and 4He source-term uncertainty, supports the argument for multi-tracer suites rather than reliance on any single tracer (Bartyzel & Różański, 2016; Okofo et al., 2022; Purtschert et al., 2022).

**3.5 Lumped Parameter Models and Tracer Input Functions**

Lumped parameter models (LPMs) are the standard interpretive bridge between measured tracer concentrations and groundwater age distributions. Rather than resolving the spatial distribution of flow within an aquifer, LPMs characterise the entire aquifer or contributing domain as a single reservoir with an idealised mixing geometry, and predict the output tracer concentration by convolving the tracer's atmospheric input function with a prescribed RTD kernel (Turnadge & Smerdon, 2014; Ma et al., 2019). The four most widely applied LPM kernels are the piston-flow model, which treats all water as arriving at identical age; the exponential model, which describes complete mixing of waters from a recharge zone with exponentially distributed ages; the dispersion model, which introduces a Péclet-number parameter to control the spread around a mean travel time; and the binary-mixing model, which represents two discrete end-members, typically young and old water, combined in variable proportions (Rädle et al., 2022; Gil-Márquez et al., 2020). In practice, most aquifer systems require at least a dispersion or binary-mixing representation because field observations consistently show that groundwater samples combine water from multiple ages, and that piston-flow ages systematically underestimate the contribution of old water fractions (Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022; Broers et al., 2021).

Input function reconstruction introduces a further source of uncertainty. For atmospheric tracers such as CFCs, SF6, and 3H, the historical atmospheric record must be adjusted for altitude, salinity, excess air, recharge temperature, and, for gas tracers, possible unsaturated-zone delay (Bartyzel & Różański, 2016; Ma et al., 2019). Recharge history assumptions, including whether recharge has been steady, whether episodic paleo-recharge under different climatic conditions contributed, and whether local point recharge differs from diffuse recharge, can shift estimated MRT by decades to millennia (Noyes et al., 2025; Cartwright et al., 2019). Model selection interacts with these input uncertainties: in a karst aquifer in southern Spain, piston-flow and exponential models gave decadal ages from CFC-12 and 3H/3He, whereas a mixing model accounting for radiogenic 4He revealed an older component of approximately 160–220 years that was invisible to young-tracer analysis alone (Gil-Márquez et al., 2020). Bayesian multi-tracer LPM approaches represent the current methodological frontier, allowing uncertainty in model type, input functions, tracer error, and mixing structure to be jointly propagated into probabilistic age distributions (Rädle et al., 2022; Thiros et al., 2023).

**3.6 Uncertainty, Ambiguity and Mixed-Age Groundwater**

Uncertainty in isotope-based groundwater age estimation arises from multiple interacting sources that are rarely quantified individually and almost never propagated jointly in the published literature. Measurement error in tracer concentrations is one source, but is typically the smallest contribution. More significant are structural uncertainties arising from model selection, because different LPM kernels imply different age distributions and there is usually no independent criterion for choosing among them (Turnadge & Smerdon, 2014; Koh et al., 2018). Tracer-specific biases represent a third source: 14C ages depend critically on the geochemical correction model chosen; SF6 ages may be inflated by terrigenic enrichment; CFC ages may be distorted by anaerobic degradation; and 3H/3He ages are sensitive to the assumed terrigenic helium component (Seltzer et al., 2021; Okofo et al., 2022; Gil-Márquez et al., 2020). Mixed-age groundwater, where a sample integrates contributions from multiple flow paths or aquifer units spanning a wide age range, represents the most fundamental source of ambiguity because no single tracer can unambiguously resolve the full RTD of such a mixture. This leads to profound equifinality, where multiple, distinct age distributions can successfully reproduce the identical observed tracer concentrations (McCallum et al., 2015, 2017; Broers et al., 2021). In fractured aquifers, for example, young water moving rapidly through open fractures mixes with old water diffusing slowly from the low-permeability matrix, producing bimodal age distributions that single-tracer methods misrepresent as intermediate ages (Meyzonnat et al., 2023).

Sampling design compounds these ambiguities. Long screened intervals integrate water from multiple hydrogeological units and flow zones, preventing depth-resolved age interpretation; in many data-limited settings, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, the available monitoring infrastructure consists predominantly of long-screened production wells that mix shallow and deep contributions (Cartwright et al., 2019; Broers et al., 2021; Banks et al., 2020). The practical consequence is that tracer-based age estimates from many such settings should be interpreted as broad indicative residence-time classes, namely modern, intermediate, or fossil, rather than as precise ages with quantified uncertainty bounds (Borzí, 2025).

**3.7 Strengths and Limitations in Data-Limited Settings**

Despite the uncertainties outlined in Section 3.6, isotope-based residence-time methods retain substantial value in data-limited aquifer settings because they provide temporal information that is entirely unavailable from conventional hydrochemical monitoring. Environmental tracers can identify whether groundwater is renewable on management timescales or represents non-renewable fossil storage, reveal hidden mixing between young contaminated and old aquifer water, and provide the independent time-scale evidence needed to constrain conceptual flow models where hydraulic head records and pumping tests are absent (Banks et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019; Aladejana et al., 2020). Their principal limitation in data-limited settings is the logistical and financial cost of sampling and analysis, the absence of robust local atmospheric input functions for bomb-pulse tracers, and the difficulty of obtaining the multi-tracer datasets, including noble gases, δ13C, DIC, and age-range-appropriate isotopes. That are necessary for credible mixed-age interpretation (Borzí, 2025; Beyene et al., 2023). A minimum defensible multi-tracer package for such settings, comprising at least one young-water indicator (3H or CFC), one old-water indicator (14C with δ13C), stable water isotopes, field parameters, and major ions, combined with well construction metadata, is discussed in the context of integrated workflows in Section 6\.

**4\. Graph Topology in Groundwater Systems**

**4.1 Aquifers as Spatial Networks of Nodes and Edges**

Graph theory provides a concise mathematical language for representing the connectivity structure of aquifer systems. In the groundwater context, nodes represent discrete hydrogeological entities (wells, springs, sinkholes, conduit junctions, recharge zones, discharge points, model cells, or groundwater-level monitoring sites), while edges represent actual or hypothesised hydraulic connections between those entities (Bodin et al., 2021; Taccari et al., 2024). Edge weights encode the strength or character of those connections and may represent hydraulic conductance, distance, travel-time cost, tracer-inferred connection probability, or model-derived particle flux, depending on the type of graph and the available data (Kanavas et al., 2021; Schiavo et al., 2022). In karst and fractured-rock aquifers, where water moves primarily through discrete conduits and fracture networks, the graph representation is physically intuitive: conduit junctions are nodes and individual conduit segments are edges, with their hydraulic properties encoded as weights (Malenica et al., 2018; Gouy et al., 2024). In porous aquifers, where flow is spatially distributed, graphs more commonly represent monitoring networks, model cell clusters, or data-driven spatial dependencies inferred from correlations among groundwater-level time series, an area where Graph Neural Networks have recently advanced the state-of-the-art for predicting hydraulic behavior in sparse-data conditions (Zhong et al., 2023; Taccari et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024).

Graph-based representations offer several specific advantages for data-limited settings. They can integrate heterogeneous information types (piezometric heads, geological maps, tracer test results, geophysical profiles, and hydrochemical clustering outputs) into a unified connectivity structure that can be updated incrementally as new data become available (Dwivedi et al., 2025; Borzí, 2025). Global graph metrics, including path length, betweenness centrality, clustering coefficient, and community structure, can highlight critical hydraulic connections, barriers, and potential recharge-discharge communities in ways that are not immediately evident from point data or spatial interpolations (Yu et al., 2024). The conceptual relationship between graph topology, isotope residence time, and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling is illustrated in Figure 1 and Figure 3\.

**4.2 Graph-Based Flow-Path Approximation and Particle-Tracking Benchmarks**

Graph-based models approximate full numerical groundwater-flow simulations by representing the aquifer domain as a network of nodes connected by conductance-weighted edges, then solving for flow through the network using Kirchhoff-type equations rather than full partial differential equations. In discrete fracture network (DFN) models, this approximation has been rigorously benchmarked: Karra et al. (2017) demonstrated that graph-based flow calculations were approximately 10,000 times faster than high-fidelity DFN simulations, with corrected graph transport times matching full breakthrough curves after accounting for in-plane flow correction factors. Doolaeghe et al. (2020) extended this by comparing fracture-intersection graphs and conduit-segment graphs, finding that graph type strongly affected local-flow accuracy and that intersection-based graphs, when corrected, predicted heads and fluxes well for the main connected backbone of the network. Machine-learning reduction of DFNs to their hydraulically dominant backbone using graph centrality metrics preserved breakthrough curve behaviour while reducing network size to approximately 20% of the original (Valera et al., 2017).

For porous aquifers, MODFLOW/MODPATH particle tracking provides a physically based method for converting numerical flow models into directed connectivity information. Forward particle tracking maps hydraulic connections from recharge areas to wells, springs, and discharge zones, effectively generating a particle-weighted directed graph whose edge strengths encode probability of connection and travel-time distributions (Alberti et al., 2018; Gonzalez et al., 2020). Backward tracking from receptor points identifies likely source areas, while ensemble tracking across multiple calibrated parameter realisations converts these pathways into probabilistic graphs with formal uncertainty in edge direction and weight (Colombo et al., 2021; Moore et al., 2023). MODPATH travel-time distributions can be calibrated against 14C groundwater ages using inverse porosity estimation, demonstrating a direct quantitative link between particle-track-derived graph priors and environmental-tracer residence-time data (Meyer et al., 2018). This intersection, that is, the particle tracking generating graph priors that are then tested against isotope ages, is one of the key workflow elements proposed in Section 6\.

**4.3 Directed Graphs, Edge Confidence and Probabilistic Connectivity**

Groundwater flow is directional, and this directionality is a fundamental hydrogeological property that undirected graphs, which treat connections as symmetric, cannot represent. Directed graphs, in which edges carry an explicit from-node to-node orientation aligned with the hydraulic gradient, are therefore necessary for tracing recharge-to-discharge pathways, attributing contaminant sources to receptors, and constraining the sequence in which geochemical reactions occur along flow paths (Schiavo et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2019). In northern Italy, probabilistic preferential groundwater networks inferred from stochastic realisations of aquifer-bottom topography consistently aligned with observed piezometric flow directions, validating the use of gradient-based criteria for edge direction assignment (Schiavo et al., 2022). However, in settings where flow directions are transient (that is reversing seasonally, changing under pumping, or switching in karst conduits under different boundary conditions), directed edges must be treated as dynamic rather than fixed structural properties (Xu et al., 2019).

Edge confidence encodes the degree of support for any proposed connection and is essential for preventing graph topology from generating misleading interpretations. Five sources of evidence can be combined to assign edge weights: hydraulic gradient direction and magnitude, which establish which connections are energetically plausible; plausible path distance and travel time consistent with available age tracers; geochemical compatibility, meaning that connected nodes share recharge signatures, evolve along lithologically consistent reaction paths, or show consistent redox transitions; model-derived particle flux, which assigns higher weight to edges traversed by many particles; and consistency of observed age ordering along the proposed flow path, with downgradient nodes having older or mixed-older groundwater than upgradient nodes (Schiavo et al., 2022; Kanavas et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019; Starn et al., 2021). Edges supported by several independent lines of evidence simultaneously (for example, head gradient, isotope age ordering, and geochemical compatibility) should be assigned the highest confidence, while edges supported by spatial proximity alone should be treated as speculative hypotheses. An explicit probabilistic graph, in which each edge carries a numerical confidence score derived from multiple evidence types, represents the target output of the topology analysis stage in the integrated workflow described in Section 6\.

**4.4 Sheaf-Style Consistency Across Connected Observations**

Sheaf theory provides a rigorous mathematical framework for evaluating the global consistency of local observations distributed across a network. In a sheaf model, each node or edge carries a local data object (such as a vector of hydrochemical concentrations, tracer ages, or hydraulic heads) together with restriction maps that specify how those data should relate when adjacent nodes are considered connected (Robinson, 2020; Hansen & Ghrist, 2019). The sheaf is said to admit a global section when all local observations can be reconciled across the network without contradiction; the consistency radius measures how far the actual assignment is from such global consistency, converting the concept of interpretive consistency into a computable numerical quantity (Robinson, 2020). In a groundwater context, a sheaf-style consistency check asks whether the full pattern of heads, ages, stable isotopes, major ions, and redox indicators across a network of wells is simultaneously consistent with a proposed set of directed flow edges. Edges on which local data cannot be reconciled without contradiction (for example, a proposed upstream-to-downstream edge along which apparent age decreases) receive low consistency scores and should be down-weighted or rejected. Sheaf Laplacian analysis, which decomposes the consistency structure into spectral components, can identify which subregions of the network contribute most strongly to global inconsistency, thereby localising likely conceptual-model errors rather than merely flagging that a model does not fit (Hansen & Ghrist, 2019; Kvinge et al., 2021). While sheaf methods have not yet been explicitly applied to groundwater networks, their underlying consistency-checking framework is directly applicable to the multivariable graph edges described in Section 4.3 and summarised in Table 3. In this review, we treat sheaf-style consistency analysis as a transferable mathematical framework rather than an established groundwater-network methodology. Its potential value lies in testing whether local observations of hydraulic head, groundwater age, geochemistry, and redox state are mutually consistent across hypothesised graph connections. However, because formal sheaf implementations have not yet been demonstrated for groundwater systems, this approach should be regarded as a prospective research direction requiring further computational development and field-based validation

**4.5 Difference Between Geographic Graphs, Chemical-Reaction Graphs and Statistical Correlation Graphs**

A critical but frequently overlooked distinction separates three types of graphs that appear in the groundwater literature. Geographic graphs connect nodes based on spatial proximity or physical hydraulic structure: edges represent inferred flow paths, conduit links, or shared aquifer compartments, and are constrained by head gradients, geology, tracer tests, and geophysical surveys (Schiavo et al., 2022; Fandel et al., 2022). Chemical-reaction graphs represent the network of reactions that transform an initial water into an observed final water along a flow path: nodes are chemical species or mineral phases, and edges represent forward or reverse reaction processes (Gastmans et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2020). These graphs underlie PHREEQC and NETPATH inverse modelling but are rarely drawn explicitly. Statistical correlation graphs connect wells or sampling points based on the similarity of their hydrochemical or isotopic compositions, using Pearson correlation, hydrochemical distance, PCA-based proximity, or HCA linkage (Tziritis et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020). The three graph types encode fundamentally different information: a geographic edge implies hydraulic connection; a chemical-reaction edge implies geochemical process; and a statistical edge implies compositional similarity, which may or may not reflect physical flow connection. For flow-path inference, only graphs whose edges are supported by hydraulic gradients, tracer tests, geophysical continuity, MODPATH particle tracks, mapped conduits or fractures, or independently justified hydrostratigraphy should be treated as physically admissible hydraulic graphs. Statistical similarity graphs, graph neural network adjacency matrices and chemical-reaction graphs may generate hypotheses or support hydrochemical grouping, but they should not be interpreted as groundwater-flow pathways unless independently validated by hydraulic, tracer or geological evidence. Conflating these three graph types is a common source of interpretive error in hydrogeochemical studies. A robust integrated framework must keep these distinct, using statistical graphs to identify candidate hydrochemical communities, geographic graphs to constrain plausible flow connections, and reaction graphs to test which mineral and mixing processes explain observed chemistry changes along those connections (Tziritis et al., 2023; Manu et al., 2023).

**4.6 Risks of Graph Oversimplification in Heterogeneous Aquifers**

Reducing a complex aquifer to a sparse graph of nodes and edges necessarily discards hydrogeological information. Key limitations include the exclusion of three-dimensional vertical heterogeneity in lithology and hydraulic conductivity, the effects of anisotropy whereby a pathway may be geometrically accessible yet hydraulically insignificant in the cross-gradient direction, transient stresses from pumping, recharge events, and tidal forcing that modify edge direction and weight through time, and an unresolved distinction between purely geometric connectivity within a graph and true hydraulic activity, defined by whether water exchange is occurring under current conditions (Hoque & Burgess, 2020; Costall et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2019). These risks are greatest in heterogeneous sedimentary aquifers with complex stratigraphy, in deep fractured crystalline aquifers where the active fracture population is a small fraction of all mapped fractures, and in coastal aquifers where density-driven flow reverses during tidal cycles or pumping events (Costall et al., 2020; Van Riet et al., 2022). Safeguards include using stochastic graph ensembles rather than a single deterministic network, explicitly validating graph edges against tracer tests and geophysical data, coupling graph topology with process-based flow and transport equations where physics matter, and reporting hydrogeological information lost in the graph abstraction alongside interpretive conclusions (Fandel et al., 2022; Bodin et al., 2021; Gouy et al., 2024).

**5\. Inverse Hydrogeochemistry and Reaction-Pathway Diagnosis**

**5.1 Conventional Hydrochemical Interpretation and Its Limitations**

Conventional hydrochemical interpretation of groundwater relies on field-measurable parameters (EC, pH, temperature, DO, Eh), major-ion facies analysis using Piper and Stiff diagrams, hydrochemical classification schemes, ionic ratio plots, Gibbs diagrams, and saturation index calculations (Tziritis et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2025). These tools have the advantage of requiring relatively low-cost and widely available analytical infrastructure and have generated substantial insights into hydrochemical processes across diverse aquifer types. Their fundamental limitation is that conventional analysis is essentially synchronic: it characterises the chemical state at a sampling point at one moment in time and can identify which chemical processes are thermodynamically plausible at that location, but cannot directly reconstruct the sequence of processes that occurred along the flow path to produce the observed composition. Without independent information on flow path structure, travel time, and the identity of initial waters, the interpretation of a given hydrochemical facies remains ambiguous: a Na-Cl water could reflect seawater mixing, halite dissolution, or cation exchange from a Ca-Cl or Ca-HCO3 precursor; distinguishing among these requires knowing which waters are connected, in what proportions, and over what timeframe (Tziritis et al., 2023; Slimani et al., 2017). In data-limited settings, where spatial coverage is sparse and temporal records are absent, conventional hydrochemical analysis is often the only available tool, but its non-uniqueness is maximised precisely where supporting data are fewest (Borzí, 2025; Manu et al., 2023).

**5.2 Mass-Balance Inverse Modelling with PHREEQC and NETPATH**

PHREEQC and NETPATH-WIN are the two most widely applied codes for mass-balance inverse hydrogeochemical modelling. Both operate on the same fundamental principle: they take an initial water composition and a final water composition assumed to represent an upgradient–downgradient pair along a flow path, and find combinations of mineral dissolution, mineral precipitation, gas exchange, ion exchange, redox reactions, and mixing with one or more additional end-members that simultaneously satisfy all measured major-ion concentration differences within specified uncertainty tolerances (Parkhurst & Appelo, 2013; Roy et al., 2020; Gastmans et al., 2016; Akpataku et al., 2019). PHREEQC typically combines saturation index calculations, which screen which mineral phases are thermodynamically supersaturated or undersaturated and thus candidates for precipitation or dissolution, with inverse model runs that compute mass transfer for a user-specified set of candidate phases (Guo et al., 2025; Jagert et al., 2023). NETPATH and its successor NETPATH-WIN are particularly suited to multi-isotope-constrained mass-balance modelling, and have been applied extensively to coupled carbon-isotope and major-ion interpretation in arid and semi-arid settings (Masoud et al., 2025; Srour et al., 2022; Akpataku et al., 2019).

Across a broad range of case studies, the dominant processes identified by PHREEQC and NETPATH include silicate weathering and secondary mineral precipitation in basement and crystalline aquifers; carbonate and gypsum dissolution with calcite precipitation and dedolomitisation in sedimentary carbonate-evaporite systems; cation exchange driving transitions from Ca-Mg-HCO3 to Na-rich facies; and redox-driven reactions including pyrite oxidation, sulphate reduction, iron mobilisation, and methanogenesis in deeper confined or reducing aquifer environments (Gastmans et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2020; Ghalib et al., 2020; Rafiq et al., 2022). In MAR settings, PHREEQC inverse models have been applied to quantify oxygen consumption, carbonate dissolution, and arsenic and manganese mobilisation as recharged surface water equilibrates with aquifer material (Rafiq et al., 2022). Despite their wide application, both PHREEQC and NETPATH share the limitation that they are applied to user-selected initial–final water pairs, and that their outputs are only as reliable as the assumed flow-path structure. This flow-path dependence is the central weakness addressed by the graph-constrained workflows described in Section 6\.

**5.3 Thermodynamic Constraints and Saturation-Index Logic**

Saturation indices (SI) represent the logarithm of the ratio of the ion activity product to the thermodynamic equilibrium constant for a given mineral phase; values close to zero indicate equilibrium, values greater than zero indicate supersaturation (potential precipitation), and values less than zero indicate undersaturation (potential dissolution). Saturation-index logic constrains inverse modelling by restricting mineral phase lists to those that are thermodynamically active (dissolving or precipitating) under the observed water chemistry, and by rejecting proposed reactions that imply dissolution of supersaturated phases or precipitation of undersaturated ones (Guo et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2018; Pérez-Ceballos et al., 2021). This thermodynamic filter substantially reduces the number of plausible reaction combinations and thereby partially controls non-uniqueness. However, saturation indices calculate thermodynamic equilibrium potential, not kinetic reaction rate, and a phase may be thermodynamically active at a given SI value but kinetically unreactive on the timescale of groundwater residence in a particular lithological setting (Blasco et al., 2019). Consequently, SI constraints are necessary but not sufficient: they screen implausible reactions but cannot independently identify which thermodynamically possible reactions actually occurred. They perform best when combined with mineralogical field observations (like rock core analysis, X-ray diffraction of aquifer sediments, or literature descriptions of expected mineral assemblages) that confirm the physical presence of candidate phases and thereby further constrain the inverse model (Manu et al., 2023; Jagert et al., 2023).

**5.4 Sparse Inverse Reaction Fitting and Non-Uniqueness Control**

The non-uniqueness problem in inverse hydrogeochemical modelling arises from mathematical over-parameterisation: there are typically more candidate phases and process combinations than independent constraints provided by the measured major-ion chemistry of two water samples. Different mineral assemblages namely those involving different combinations of silicates, carbonates, sulphates, exchange phases, and gas exchange, can produce equally valid mass-balance solutions (Pérez-Ceballos et al., 2021; Chakraborty et al., 2022). This ambiguity is compounded when flow paths are uncertain, when mixing dilutes reaction signals, when anthropogenic inputs mimic natural geochemical processes, or when redox-sensitive species such as arsenic, manganese, and iron are involved (Chakraborty et al., 2022; Hayford & Datta, 2021; Song et al., 2024).

Sparse inverse reaction fitting addresses non-uniqueness by deliberately restricting the candidate phase list to the smallest set of geologically and thermodynamically plausible reactions, rather than allowing an unconstrained search across all possible phases. In a combinatorial inverse modelling approach applied to the Pra Basin, Ghana, systematic testing of all plausible mineral assemblages derived from local field mineralogy identified a limited set of silicate-weathering reactions that explained basin-scale groundwater composition, demonstrating that sparse, constrained models are both computationally tractable and more interpretively credible than unconstrained models (Manu et al., 2023). Coupling sparse inverse fitting with multivariate statistical grouping (for example hierarchical cluster analysis and principal components analysis) reduces further non-uniqueness by defining hydrochemical communities that share likely recharge sources and flow conditions, and by restricting inverse model runs to within-group or between-group comparisons that represent plausible upgradient–downgradient pairs (Roy et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020). The remaining irreducible non-uniqueness (where multiple reaction sets satisfy the data even after maximum constraint) should be explicitly reported by presenting all viable model solutions alongside the criteria used to rank their plausibility, rather than reporting only the preferred model (Manu et al., 2023; Pérez-Ceballos et al., 2021).

**5.5 Coupling Nitrate, Fluoride, Salinity and Redox Processes to Residence Time**

Inverse hydrogeochemical modelling becomes significantly more diagnostic when combined with residence-time information because temporal context transforms a static mass-balance equation into a rate-constrained reaction pathway. The classic interpretive benefit is illustrated by nitrate: high nitrate in young groundwater (as evidenced by measurable 3H, CFC, or SF6 signatures) signals recent anthropogenic loading from fertiliser, manure, or wastewater, while declining nitrate with enriched δ15N and δ18O–NO3 values in older, reducing groundwater indicates progressive denitrification along the flow path, a geochemical process that is temporally linked to residence time (Biddau et al., 2019; Gerber et al., 2018). Similarly, fluoride enrichment in groundwater is primarily a geogenic process reflecting progressive dissolution of fluorapatite and fluorite along flow paths with long residence times and high pH, whereas fluoride in young, shallow groundwater is more likely to reflect surface inputs or rapid dissolution of volcanic materials (Ijumulana et al., 2021; Shube et al., 2024). Salinity in deep or confined groundwater commonly represents long-term evaporite dissolution, cation exchange, and density-driven upwelling of formation brines (processes that operate on timescales consistent with 14C or 36Cl ages) whereas salinity increases in shallow or young groundwater more frequently indicate irrigated-water return flow, evaporative concentration, or anthropogenic contamination (Mastrocicco et al., 2020; Rivett et al., 2019). Redox evolution, including the sequential depletion of dissolved oxygen, nitrate, manganese oxide, iron oxide, and sulphate along flow paths in the expected terminal-electron-acceptor sequence, can be calibrated against residence time to infer reaction rates and identify zones of elevated geogenic metal risk, including arsenic and manganese (Richards et al., 2022; Chakraborty et al., 2022). The diagnostic combinations linking chemical signals to residence-time classes are detailed in Table 4\.

**5.6 Why Point-to-Point Inverse Modelling is Weak Under Uncertain Flow Paths**

The primary structural weakness of PHREEQC and NETPATH inverse modelling, as conventionally applied, is its dependence on the user to nominate an "initial" and "final" water pair that is assumed to represent a true hydrogeologically connected upgradient–downgradient pathway. When flow paths are uncertain (as is common in heterogeneous, poorly characterised, or data-limited aquifers) this assumption is not merely a simplification but a potential source of systematic interpretive error. Different assumed flow-path pairs produce different inverse model solutions, and it is often impossible to distinguish, from the chemistry alone, whether a mass-balance solution is correct because the pair represents a true connected path or coincidentally plausible because a different combination of reactions happens to satisfy the same equations (Tziritis et al., 2023; Manu et al., 2023). In the Ganges River aquifer system, contrasting arsenic and manganese patterns were associated with different flow-path assumptions across the hydrostratigraphic architecture, demonstrating that the inferred reaction pathways were not robust to flow-path uncertainty (Chakraborty et al., 2022). This problem is particularly acute when the physical distances between samples are large, when multiple aquifer units may contribute to a well sample, or when mixing dilutes the geochemical signal expected from any single reaction pathway. The graph-constrained approach proposed in Section 6.5 addresses this by replacing subjective pair selection with a systematic, topology-informed set of candidate edges.

**5.7 Implications for Data-Limited Aquifers**

In data-limited aquifers, the prospects for productive inverse hydrogeochemical modelling depend critically on the quality of the conceptual flow model that precedes model application. Where flow paths are essentially unknown, as in many semi-arid basement aquifers in sub-Saharan Africa, conventional point-to-point inverse modelling may produce locally plausible but globally meaningless results (Borzí, 2025). The combination of three minimum inputs (a plausible directed graph of well connections, isotope-derived residence-time classes for each node, and a constrained candidate phase list derived from regional geology and saturation-index screening) transforms the inverse model from a speculative exercise into a hypothesis-testing tool. Evidence from sparse-data settings, including the Pra Basin in Ghana, basement aquifers in Togo, and fractured sandstone aquifers in Germany, demonstrates that simplified, combinatorial inverse models applied to grouped hydrochemical data can successfully identify the dominant processes controlling water quality even with limited sample sets, provided that the reaction candidate list is tightly constrained and that all plausible solutions rather than only preferred ones are reported (Manu et al., 2023; Akpataku et al., 2019; Jagert et al., 2023).

**6\. Integrated Frameworks for Data-Limited Aquifers**

**6.1 Why Residence Time, Topology and Reaction Modelling Should Be Integrated**

Each of the three methodological domains reviewed above provides independent and largely non-overlapping information. Environmental-tracer residence time answers when groundwater was recharged and how long it has circulated, thereby indicating whether the resource is renewable on management timescales and providing the temporal axis for rate-dependent geochemical processes. Graph topology answers which sampling points or aquifer zones are likely connected, in which direction, and with what degree of confidence, thereby providing the spatial structure within which age data and chemistry data can be interpreted coherently. Inverse hydrogeochemical modelling answers what reactions and mixing proportions transform initial recharge chemistry into the observed groundwater composition, thereby providing the process mechanism that links residence time to observed water quality. No single method can substitute for another: isotope ages without flow-path structure are unlocated in space; flow-path graphs without temporal information carry no rate-constrained process evidence; and inverse models without independent flow-path and age constraints remain highly non-unique (Borzí, 2025; Tziritis et al., 2023; Starn et al., 2021).

Existing reviews and synthesis papers confirm that current practice typically treats these methods in parallel rather than in concert. Isotope and tracer reviews are paired with flow models and water budgets but rarely with graph connectivity. Inverse geochemical models are applied along assumed flow paths without independent topological constraint. Graph and network representations of aquifer systems, where they appear, seldom incorporate age or reaction information (Borzí, 2025; Banerjee et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021). The mutual-constraint benefit of integration is clearly illustrated by the Belgian Neogene aquifer study, where 3H/3He, 4He, 14C, stable isotopes, and hydrochemistry together, rather than any single tracer, were required to separate shallow-modern, deep-old, and vertically mixed groundwater systems—a result that would have been impossible without jointly interpreting age, source, and geochemical evolution (Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022). The integrated conceptual framework proposed here, summarised in Figure 1 and Table 6, extends this multi-method logic to explicitly incorporate graph topology as the structural bridge between residence time and reaction modelling.

**6.2 Public Benchmark Data: USGS Tracer Datasets, MODFLOW/MODPATH Models and IAEA Isotope Networks**

Publicly available datasets offer a tractable starting point for developing and validating integrated workflows before applying them to data-limited settings where field data are scarce. Dataset availability should not be interpreted as uniform completeness. NWIS, WISER, GNIP, ScienceBase MODFLOW/MODPATH archives and the BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas vary substantially in tracer coverage, screen-depth metadata, noble-gas availability, hydrochemical completeness, model availability and spatial density. Their main value in this review is therefore workflow development, benchmarking and transferability assessment rather than direct substitution for local field data. The USGS National Water Information System (NWIS) contains an extensive catalogue of environmental tracer measurements, including 3H, 14C, CFCs, SF6, and noble gases which are linked to well construction metadata, hydrochemical analyses, and geographical coordinates, providing multi-tracer datasets for aquifer systems ranging from the glaciated Northeast to arid basins of the Southwest (Jurgens et al., 2022; Starn et al., 2021). Many of these datasets are accompanied by MODFLOW/MODPATH model archives that provide particle-track-derived travel times and RTDs calibrated against field data, enabling direct comparison of simulated and tracer-based residence time estimates (Baker et al., 2025; Meyer et al., 2018). The IAEA Global Network of Isotopes in Precipitation (GNIP) and the associated WISER groundwater isotope database contain stable water isotope (δ2H, δ18O) and tritium data for precipitation and groundwater across more than 150 countries, providing input functions for isotope-based age modelling and recharge source characterisation in under-studied regions (Jasechko, 2019; Mohamed et al., 2021). For hydrogeochemical benchmarking, the PHREEQC and NETPATH example databases distributed with those codes provide verified input files for a range of aquifer types and reaction scenarios.
