The principal limitation of public datasets for transfer to African semi-arid settings is discussed in Section 7.5; public datasets are best used at the workflow-development and uncertainty-benchmarking stages, with local field data subsequently used to recalibrate and validate the framework. Table 5 summarises the principal public datasets identified in this review.

The practical implementation of the framework is summarised in Box 1\. The staged algorithm identifies the minimum data required at each step, the decision rules used to construct and test graph edges, the inverse-modelling outputs expected from each retained edge, and the validation checks needed before interpretations can be used for management decisions.

**Box 1\. Minimum operational algorithm for the proposed integrated workflow**

The proposed framework can be implemented as a staged workflow. First, compile node-level data, including well coordinates, screen depth, water level, field EC, pH, temperature, DO/Eh, major ions, stable isotopes and available age tracers. Second, assign each node a preliminary residence-time class, such as modern, mixed/intermediate or old/fossil, using tracer evidence and uncertainty bounds. Third, construct a candidate directed graph in which nodes represent wells, springs, recharge zones or model cells, and edges represent plausible flow connections inferred from hydraulic gradients, geology, distance, tracer evidence and available particle tracks. Fourth, score edge confidence using agreement among head gradients, age ordering, geochemical compatibility, lithological plausibility and model support. Fifth, screen graph consistency by flagging edges where downgradient age, redox state or chemistry contradict expected flow-path evolution, while recognising that mixed wells, long screens or local recharge may also explain apparent inconsistency. Sixth, run inverse hydrogeochemical models only on graph-supported initial–final water pairs, using phase lists constrained by mineralogy, saturation indices and redox state. Seventh, report all viable reaction solutions satisfying mass balance and thermodynamic constraints, and rank them by residuals, phase plausibility and agreement with age-derived reaction windows. Eighth, propagate uncertainty by repeating the analysis across alternative age models, graph realisations and phase lists. Finally, validate interpretations where possible using withheld wells, repeat sampling, geophysics, tracer tests, independent head data or calibrated numerical models.

**6.3 Workflow 1: Environmental-Isotopes Tracer Age Inference Constrained by Graph Topology**

The first workflow uses graph topology to constrain and validate isotope-based age interpretations. In this workflow, apparent ages derived from LPM analysis of 3H, 3H/3He, 14C, or complementary tracers are plotted as node attributes on a directed graph whose edges have been assigned from hydraulic gradients, geological connectivity, tracer evidence, and MODPATH particle tracks. The primary quality test is whether apparent age increases monotonically from upgradient to downgradient nodes along the directed edges: age consistency with the proposed flow direction is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for edge credibility (Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2019). Where age ordering is inconsistent with a proposed edge, for example, where a downgradient node appears younger than an upgradient node without any evidence of mixing or local recharge, that edge should be down-weighted or rejected, and the inconsistency should be documented in a sheaf-style consistency score for the full graph (Robinson, 2020; Hansen & Ghrist, 2019). Where age inconsistencies persist despite edge revision, they signal either mixed-age groundwater (requiring multi-tracer TTD analysis rather than single-tracer apparent ages), wrong connectivity assumptions (requiring hydrogeological reinterpretation), or local recharge inputs along the flow path not represented in the graph structure (Atencio et al., 2024; Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022). This workflow does not require a MODFLOW model: a simple directed graph constructed from hydraulic head contours, geological knowledge, and hydrochemical facies grouping is sufficient to test age-ordering consistency, as demonstrated by studies in Morocco, sub-Saharan Africa, and West Africa that used similar integrative logic even without formal graph notation (Hssaisoune et al., 2022; Banks et al., 2020; Kpegli et al., 2018).

**6.4 Workflow 2: MODPATH-Informed Graph Priors for Residence-Time and Reaction Modelling**

The second workflow uses MODPATH particle-tracking outputs from publicly available or locally calibrated MODFLOW models to generate formal graph priors for subsequent age and reaction modelling. Particle tracks are translated into directed graph edges by identifying recurring source-to-receptor pathways, with edge weights defined by particle-crossing frequency to represent hydraulic flux along each path and temporal attributes derived from the distribution of particle travel times associated with each edge (Alberti et al., 2018; Starn et al., 2021; Gonzalez et al., 2020). These particle-track-derived graph priors serve two constraining functions: first, they restrict the allowable connectivity structure for LPM analysis by specifying which wells or springs are hydraulically connected and at what travel-time scale, thereby directly constraining the feasible LPM parameter space; second, they restrict inverse geochemical model runs to upgradient–downgradient pairs that are hydraulically supported by the particle track structure, eliminating the arbitrary pair selection that underlies conventional point-to-point inverse modelling (Meyer et al., 2018; Starn & Belitz, 2018). Where public MODFLOW models are unavailable, the workflow can be initiated using simplified analytical flow models, such as radial or regional Dupuit solutions, to approximate particle trajectories and provide first-order connectivity priors that can be progressively refined as local data become available (Borzí, 2025).

**6.5 Workflow 3: Inverse Hydrogeochemical Fitting Along Graph Edges**

The third workflow applies inverse hydrogeochemical modelling directly along the graph edges defined in Workflows 1 and 2, rather than to arbitrarily selected sample pairs. Each directed edge connects a specific initial-water node to a final-water node whose hydrochemical compositions are measured, and the mass-balance inverse model is applied to reconstruct the reaction pathway along that edge. Candidate phase lists for each edge are constrained by the SI of the initial water, the known mineralogy or geological description of the aquifer material traversed by that edge, and the redox state inferred from field measurements (Manu et al., 2023; Jagert et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2025). Residence-time priors from Workflows 1 or 2 constrain the reaction time available along each edge, which indirectly limits plausible mass-transfer magnitudes by disallowing reactions whose stoichiometric requirements imply mineral exposure times inconsistent with the inferred age difference between nodes (Ameli et al., 2017). By running inverse models systematically across all graph edges, rather than only a small number of manually selected pairs, the workflow generates a comprehensive inventory of reactions and their mass-transfer magnitudes across the spatial network, allows cross-edge comparison of mass-balance residuals to identify inconsistent edges, and produces a spatially distributed picture of geochemical evolution that can be validated against regional mineralogical data and water-quality maps (Tziritis et al., 2023; Manu et al., 2023). The output is a network-scale geochemical process map rather than a point-scale process diagnosis, as illustrated conceptually in Figure 3 and Figure 6\.

**6.6 Workflow 4: Uncertainty Propagation Across Age, Topology and Reaction Terms**

The fourth workflow is explicitly a meta-workflow that propagates uncertainty from each of the three methodological domains, namely isotope-based age estimation, graph topology, and inverse reaction modelling, through the integrated framework to produce a probabilistic diagnostic output. This requires explicit treatment of three sources of structured uncertainty. First, isotope age uncertainty arises from measurement error, LPM model selection, input function reconstruction, and tracer-specific bias; Monte Carlo sampling across these dimensions generates an ensemble of age distributions for each node (Thiros et al., 2023; Rädle et al., 2022). Second, graph topology uncertainty arises from incomplete knowledge of hydraulic connectivity, edge direction, and edge weight; stochastic graph ensembles where edge probabilities are sampled from their confidence distributions generate a range of possible network structures (Schiavo et al., 2022; Banusch et al., 2022). Third, inverse model uncertainty arises from phase-list selection, mass-balance tolerance settings, and the non-uniqueness of multiple viable reaction solutions; reporting all viable solutions rather than a preferred single model quantifies this dimension (Pérez-Ceballos et al., 2021; Manu et al., 2023). Bayesian frameworks that update prior probability distributions over flow-path structure and reaction parameters as new observations become available offer a principled mechanism for combining these uncertainty sources and reducing them incrementally as data are added. Bayesian Model Averaging offers a particularly robust mechanism in this regard for resolving conceptual equifinality among competing flow paths and reaction models (Wöhling et al., 2018; Gonzalez et al., 2020; Thiros et al., 2023; Schiavo et al., 2023). This fourth workflow translates the integrated method into a probabilistic diagnostic map that provides a spatial representation of confidence in recharge source, flow connectivity, geochemical processes, and water-quality risk, making it directly useful for management decisions under data limitation.

**6.7 Proposed Evaluation Metrics for Integrated Frameworks**

Evaluating the performance of integrated frameworks requires metrics specific to each methodological component and at least one metric addressing integration quality. For isotope-based age, evaluation metrics include the model efficiency statistic comparing LPM-predicted tracer concentrations against measured values, the coverage probability of the age uncertainty interval, and the agreement between age ordering predicted by the graph and observed apparent ages at connected nodes. For graph topology, relevant metrics include the fraction of proposed edges that are directionally consistent with observed hydraulic head gradients; the edge-consistency score derived from the sheaf-style analysis of age, chemistry, and redox patterns across each edge; and the correlation between particle-track-weighted edge probabilities and tracer-based transit-time estimates. For inverse hydrogeochemical modelling, metrics include the mass-balance residual per constrained species across each edge, the fraction of viable reaction solutions that are consistent with independent SI screening and field mineralogy, and the reduction in the number of equally plausible reaction sets achieved by graph constraint relative to unconstrained pair selection. An integration quality metric that evaluates the fraction of individual method outputs that remain consistent across the fully integrated framework provides an overall indicator of whether the three domains yield mutually reinforcing or internally contradictory diagnoses. Table 6 organises these metrics alongside the research gaps they are designed to address.

**7\. Discussion**

**7.1 What Current Methods Already Solve Well**

Environmental-tracer methods are already well suited to binary age classification (distinguishing modern, post-bomb groundwater from pre-modern groundwater) and to residence-time estimation in relatively simple, young, shallow aquifer systems where single-tracer LPMs are reliable and mixing is limited. The 3H/3He method, in particular, provides robust apparent ages for groundwater less than approximately 70 years old in unconfined aquifers with low terrigenic helium, and case studies from alluvial aquifers in North America, Europe, and South Africa demonstrate consistent, field-validated results where the required noble-gas dataset is available (Gilmore et al., 2021; Newman et al., 2021; Van Rooyen et al., 2020). Carbon-14 dating, when properly corrected using the statistical 14C–δ13C approach or full geochemical mass-balance models, reliably distinguishes Holocene from Pleistocene groundwater in confined sedimentary systems, supporting palaeohydrological reconstructions and fossil-resource assessments (Cartwright et al., 2019; Martínez et al., 2025).

Numerical groundwater modelling combined with MODPATH particle tracking is already mature for capture-zone delineation, source-receptor pathway screening, and stream-aquifer exchange characterisation in well-parameterised systems (Gonzalez et al., 2020; Starn et al., 2021). PHREEQC and NETPATH inverse modelling reliably reconstruct dominant reaction pathways (for example, silicate weathering, carbonate dissolution, cation exchange, evaporite dissolution) in chemically simple or moderately complex aquifer systems where the assumed flow path is well supported by independent hydraulic evidence and the mineralogy is locally constrained (Roy et al., 2020; Gastmans et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2025). Multivariate statistical methods including PCA and HCA provide effective hydrochemical grouping as a precursor to inverse modelling, particularly when combined with saturation-index screening (Tziritis et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020).

**7.2 Major Unresolved Gaps: Age Ambiguity, Topology Uncertainty and Reaction Non-Uniqueness**

The three primary unresolved gaps in the literature map directly onto the three methodological domains reviewed. Age ambiguity is the inability to uniquely resolve the RTD of a groundwater sample from available tracer data, arising from mixing, dispersion, non-piston flow, incomplete input function knowledge, and tracer-specific biases that each distort the tracer signal relative to the true physical residence time (Benettin et al., 2022; Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022; Broers et al., 2021). The gap is particularly acute for intermediate-age groundwater in the range of approximately 100 to 10,000 years, where 3H and 3H/3He have fully decayed, 14C corrections carry large uncertainties, and intermediate-age tracers such as 39Ar and 85Kr require analytical infrastructure available only at a few specialised laboratories worldwide (Broers et al., 2021; Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022). In data-limited settings, the probability of having even a two-tracer dataset spanning this range is low.

Topology uncertainty is the inability to determine, from available field data, which wells or aquifer zones are genuinely hydraulically connected, in what direction, and at what travel-time scale. This uncertainty is maximised in heterogeneous aquifers with complex three-dimensional stratigraphy, faulting, or fracture networks, and in settings where piezometric head records are sparse or absent (Borzí, 2025; Hoque & Burgess, 2020). Current practice typically resolves this ambiguity through informal expert judgement, that is , the hydrogeologist selects a flow path based on experience and available data, rather than through formal probabilistic or quantitative methods. The consequence is that subjective flow-path selection propagates unquantified uncertainty into all downstream isotope age interpretation and inverse geochemical modelling (Tziritis et al., 2023; Chakraborty et al., 2022).

Reaction non-uniqueness is the inability to uniquely identify, from observed mass-balance constraints, which combination of mineral reactions and mixing processes transformed initial recharge water into observed groundwater chemistry. Even with SI screening and sparse fitting, multiple reaction assemblages can satisfy all available constraints, and the non-uniqueness grows with increasing geochemical complexity, uncertain flow paths, and decreasing sample size (Pérez-Ceballos et al., 2021; Manu et al., 2023; Hayford & Datta, 2021). These three gaps are not independent: age ambiguity limits the temporal constraint on reaction kinetics; topology uncertainty makes flow-path-dependent reaction models contingent on assumptions that may be wrong; and reaction non-uniqueness prevents geochemical evidence from validating or rejecting topology assumptions with the confidence that would be needed to resolve age ambiguity. Addressing all three simultaneously, which is the objective of the integrated framework proposed in Section 6, requires methodological advances described in Section 7.6.

However, the proposed integration can fail in diagnostically ambiguous ways. Apparent age reversal along a graph edge does not necessarily prove that the edge is wrong; it may reflect mixed-age pumping from long screens, local recharge between nodes, tracer-specific bias, geochemical alteration of 14C, terrigenic helium effects, pumping-induced vertical leakage or seasonal gradient reversal. Similarly, a successful inverse geochemical mass balance does not prove hydraulic connection unless the edge is independently supported. Integrated workflows should therefore treat contradictions as triggers for alternative hypotheses rather than as automatic rejection criteria.

**7.3 How Graph-Constrained Methods Can Reduce Subjective Flow-Path Selection**

In conventional practice, groundwater flow-path selection for inverse geochemical modelling proceeds through informal interpretation: the hydrogeologist nominates an upgradient sample as "initial water" and a downgradient sample as "final water" based on piezometric head contours, conceptual aquifer diagrams, and chemistry similarity, without a formal record of why other candidate pairs were rejected (Tziritis et al., 2023; Camara et al., 2024). This subjectivity is consequential: as Section 5.6 demonstrates, different flow-path assumptions generate different inverse model solutions, and the solution reported as "the" reaction pathway may be only one of many equally plausible alternatives. Graph-constrained connectivity replaces this subjective step with a systematic, multi-evidence framework. By requiring that proposed flow edges simultaneously satisfy hydraulic head gradients, isotope age ordering, hydrochemical compatibility, and, where available, particle-track support, graph construction imposes multiple independent tests that a flow path must pass before it is incorporated into the inverse model (Schiavo et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2019; Starn et al., 2021). Edges that pass all tests receive high confidence and are retained; edges that pass only one or two tests are assigned lower confidence and may be tested as alternative hypotheses; edges that fail multiple tests are excluded or flagged as inconsistent.

The practical consequence for inverse modelling is that the initial–final sample pairs submitted to PHREEQC or NETPATH are now defined by the graph rather than by individual expert choice, reducing the influence of any single analyst's assumptions on the reported results (Manu et al., 2023). Running the inverse model across all graph edges (including lower-confidence edges as sensitivity tests) replaces a point estimate with a distribution of mass-balance solutions whose spread reflects genuine connectivity uncertainty rather than arbitrary analyst choice. This approach is directly compatible with the combinatorial inverse modelling framework of Manu et al. (2023), the probabilistic particle-tracking frameworks of Gonzalez et al. (2020) and Colombo et al. (2021), and the LPM uncertainty analysis of Rädle et al. (2022), and represents a methodological bridge between these currently separate literatures.

**7.4 How Environmental Isotopes Tracers Improve Hydrochemical Process Interpretation**

Environmental isotopes tracers improve hydrochemical process interpretation primarily by anchoring observed chemistry to a temporal context that transforms a static water analysis into a time-resolved record of process evolution. Without temporal context, the same ion concentrations can be consistent with multiple competing process hypotheses operating at very different rates and durations; with a residence-time estimate, the suite of processes consistent with the observed chemistry is constrained to those that can proceed to the observed extent within the available time (Sakakibara et al., 2019; Lapworth et al., 2018; Moreau et al., 2019). Young water with anthropogenic tracers (nitrate, pharmaceuticals, PFAS) signals recent surface-derived contamination and rapid recharge connectivity; old water with enriched fluoride, arsenic, or salinity signals long-term geogenic water-rock interaction; and the coexistence of young tracers in deep wells signals preferential leakage pathways that depth alone cannot reveal (Lapworth et al., 2018; Siegel et al., 2022; Shube et al., 2024).

For redox-sensitive species, the coupling of residence time to reaction sequence is particularly powerful. Along flow paths from oxic recharge to anoxic deep aquifer zones, the sequential consumption of dissolved oxygen, nitrate, manganese oxide, iron oxide, and sulphate (the canonical terminal-electron-acceptor sequence) occurs on timescales that are at least partially predictable from residence time and organic carbon availability (Richards et al., 2022; Biddau et al., 2019). Tracer-constrained residence times can therefore predict which redox phase is expected at a given age, enabling the identification of anomalous geochemical signatures (arsenic or manganese concentrations inconsistent with the predicted redox zone for the apparent groundwater age) that indicate either non-equilibrium conditions, unusual mineralogy, or incorrect flow-path assumptions (Richards et al., 2022; Chakraborty et al., 2022). This predictive capability is directly relevant to water-quality risk management in data-limited settings, where geogenic contamination by fluoride, arsenic, and nitrate poses severe human health risks that conventional hydrochemical monitoring alone cannot anticipate (Nowicki et al., 2023; Bretzler et al., 2017; Ijumulana et al., 2021).

**7.5 Limits of Public Data and Transferability to African Semi-Arid Aquifers**

The public benchmark datasets described in Section 6.2, that is, USGS NWIS tracer archives, MODFLOW/MODPATH models, and IAEA isotope networks, provide invaluable resources for workflow development and uncertainty benchmarking, but their direct transferability to African semi-arid aquifers is limited by several structural factors. The USGS and related North American and European datasets were collected in well-monitored hydrogeological settings with relatively dense observation networks, long-term head records, comprehensive pumping test databases, and institutional support for specialised isotope analysis that is rarely available in sub-Saharan Africa (Borzí, 2025; Nowicki et al., 2023). The aquifer types represented, glacial sedimentary systems in the northeastern USA, alluvial basins in the western USA, chalk and limestone aquifers in Europe, which differ fundamentally in hydrogeological character from the weathered basement, fractured crystalline rock, alluvial valley, and rift-volcanic aquifer systems that dominate groundwater supply across most of sub-Saharan Africa, where groundwater resilience to climate change relies on highly localized and episodic recharge pathways (MacDonald et al., 2021; Gurmessa et al., 2022; Mudimbu et al., 2024).

Semi-arid settings introduce additional challenges that are structurally different from the humid settings that dominate the public archive literature. Episodic, focused recharge through ephemeral stream channels and fracture systems produces highly variable and often unmeasured tritium input functions; thick vadose zones introduce age lags not accounted for in standard LPMs; and the dominance of basement lithologies with limited mineralogical variability constrains which inverse model reactions are geologically plausible (Beyene et al., 2023; Van Wyk et al., 2024; Seddon et al., 2021). Institutional capacity constraints, for example, limited access to noble-gas mass spectrometry, restricted laboratory infrastructure, absence of systematic water-level monitoring, and highly variable borehole construction quality, further limit the minimum multi-tracer package that can realistically be assembled at scale in these settings (Nowicki et al., 2023; Borzí, 2025). 

In African semi-arid settings, the staged workflow should be interpreted as a feasibility ladder. Low-cost field stages include EC, pH, temperature, water level, well depth, major ions and basic facies classification. Regional laboratory stages include stable water isotopes, tritium, selected trace elements and saturation-index screening. Specialist stages include 14C, noble gases, 3H/3He, 39Ar, 85Kr and calibrated MODFLOW/MODPATH modelling. The framework therefore does not require all methods at the outset; it defines how interpretation should improve as data availability increases. Hence, adapting integrated frameworks to African contexts therefore requires not only technical recalibration of the methods but also deliberate framework design that builds from the lowest-cost and most widely available data types, before escalating to specialised tracer analysis (Cid-Escobar et al., 2023; Ferrer et al., 2019).

**7.6 Minimum Reporting Standards for Future Integrated Studies**

For studies integrating environmental-tracer residence time, graph topology, and inverse hydrogeochemistry to reach the minimum reporting standards, they must satisfy several methodological standards that are currently uncommon even in high-quality individual-method studies. First, multi-tracer age estimation is required rather than single-tracer apparent ages: at minimum, two tracers with overlapping but distinct residence-time windows should be combined within a formal LPM or Bayesian age-distribution framework, and the age uncertainty should be explicitly quantified and reported (Rädle et al., 2022; Thiros et al., 2023). Second, connectivity should be established through formal graph construction using explicitly stated and justified criteria for node definition, edge direction, edge weight, and edge confidence, rather than through informal flow path selection, and the sensitivity of inverse model outputs to graph uncertainty should be explicitly tested (Schiavo et al., 2022; Manu et al., 2023). Third, inverse hydrogeochemical models should report all viable reaction solutions alongside the criteria for ranking them, should explicitly constrain phase lists against SI calculations and local mineralogy, and should document rejected models to enable independent reproducibility assessment (Pérez-Ceballos et al., 2021; Manu et al., 2023). Fourth, the overall framework must include a formal uncertainty propagation step that translates uncertainties in age estimation, topology, and reaction modelling into confidence bounds on the final diagnostic outputs, such as vulnerability classifications, source attributions, or process maps, using Monte Carlo, Bayesian, or ensemble approaches (Gonzalez et al., 2020; Schiavo et al., 2023). Finally, independent validation using withheld well data, repeat seasonal sampling, independent geophysical surveys, or comparison with a calibrated numerical model should be performed and reported, even if limited in scale (Borzí, 2025).

**7.7 Critical Synthesis and Research Agenda**

The fundamental intellectual contribution of integrating environmental-tracer residence time, graph topology, and inverse hydrogeochemistry is that it provides a physically consistent and progressively constrained framework for diagnosing the temporal, spatial, and process dimensions of groundwater systems simultaneously. Each methodological strand addresses a different dimension of what might be called the groundwater-system triplet: when did water recharge and how long has it circulated; which parts of the aquifer are connected and in what direction; and what reactions have transformed recharge water into observed groundwater chemistry. When treated separately, each strand is vulnerable to non-uniqueness and bias from the other two unknown dimensions. When integrated particularly with isotope ages constraining graph edge plausibility, graph topology constraining inverse model pair selection, and inverse model reaction rates constrained by age-derived reaction times. The three dimensions mutually constrain each other, systematically reducing non-uniqueness in ways that no single method can achieve alone (Borzí, 2025; Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022; Starn et al., 2021). The highest-priority research needs arising from this synthesis are: development of intermediate-age tracer capabilities (39Ar, 85Kr) at scale; formal probabilistic graph construction methods that can operate from sparse field data without MODFLOW models; and open-source software workflows that implement edge-constrained combinatorial inverse modelling with explicit uncertainty propagation, applied to benchmark public datasets and subsequently to African semi-arid aquifer test cases.

However, outputs from the integrated framework should be classified according to evidential maturity. Interpretations supported only by single-campaign hydrochemistry or unvalidated graph assumptions should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Outputs supported by repeated sampling, independent tracer evidence, geophysics or hydraulic validation may be used for decision support with stated uncertainty. Only interpretations validated by independent data and sensitivity analysis should be treated as management-ready.

**8\. Conclusions**

This review argues that data-limited aquifer interpretation remains non-unique when groundwater residence time, hydraulic connectivity and hydrogeochemical reactions are evaluated separately. Isotope and environmental tracers constrain when groundwater recharged and whether it is modern, mixed or old; graph topology constrains where water may move and which nodes are hydraulically connected; and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling constrains what reactions and mixing processes can explain observed chemistry. The proposed contribution is therefore conceptual and methodological: a staged framework in which age classes constrain graph edges, graph topology guides inverse-model pair selection, and reaction models are filtered by mineralogy, saturation indices and residence-time evidence.

The framework is not yet a validated field tool. It requires software implementation, benchmark testing and application to real aquifer datasets before its uncertainty-reduction value can be demonstrated quantitatively. In data-limited regions, especially semi-arid African aquifers, implementation should begin with low-cost hydrochemistry, well metadata, water levels and stable isotopes, then add tritium, 14C, noble gases, 3H/3He, 39Ar or 85Kr only where laboratory access and research objectives justify the cost. Future work should prioritise transparent study matrices, reproducible graph construction, reporting of all viable inverse-model solutions and validation through repeat sampling, geophysics, tracer tests or calibrated flow models.

Figures

![][image1]

Figure 1\. Conceptual integration of environmental-tracer residence time directed graph topology and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling. Residence-time evidence constrains timing and recharge source, graph topology constrains plausible hydraulic connectivity, and inverse hydrogeochemical modelling test’s reaction and mixing processes along graph-supported edges. Uncertainty propagation and independent validation are required before the integrated diagnosis can be treated as management-ready.

![][image2]

Figure 2: Dating ranges of common groundwater tracers, demonstrating relative usefulness of 3H, 3H/3He, 85Kr, SF6, CFCs, 14C, 36Cl, 81Kr and 4He across residence-time scales.

![][image3]

Figure 3: Point-based versus graph-constrained groundwater interpretation a paired schematic on how isolated sample interpretation differs from network edge-based process inference.

![][image4]

Figure 4: Sources of uncertainty in data-limited aquifer diagnosis an uncertainty cascade diagram which demonstrates, propagation from tracer measurement, input functions, topology, geochemistry and model selection.

![][image5]

Figure 5\. Critical-review framework used to compare tracer, graph and inverse-modelling methods. The figure shows how the review moves from method-specific evidence to cross-method criteria, uncertainty diagnosis and research-gap synthesis.

![][image6]

Figure 6\. Operational workflow proposed for future studies. The workflow is staged so that low-cost field evidence can generate preliminary hypotheses, while isotope, graph and inverse-model evidence progressively increase confidence as data become available.

**Table 2\.** Comparison of groundwater-age modelling approaches.

| Model type | Input data | Key assumptions | Strengths | Limitations | Suitability for data-limited aquifers | Key references |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Piston-flow model (PFM) | Single tracer concentration; atmospheric input function or known initial activity | Water moves as a plug with no mixing; all water at a sampling point is the same age | Simple; requires minimum data; provides a single apparent age for screening | Severely biased in systems with mixing, dispersion, or heterogeneous flow; underestimates old-water fraction | Suitable only for binary young/old screening; not appropriate for detailed age characterisation | Gilmore et al. (2021); Turnadge & Smerdon (2014) |
| Exponential mixing model (EMM) | Single or two tracer concentrations; atmospheric input function | Recharge zone with fully mixed exponential age distribution; all ages from 0 to ∞ present | Captures age distribution for shallow unconfined aquifers with well-mixed recharge | Overestimates young-water fraction in confined or stratified aquifers; unrealistic for deep or heterogeneous systems | Moderate; applicable where shallow, mixed unconfined aquifers dominate | Turnadge & Smerdon (2014); Ma et al. (2019) |
| Dispersion model (DM) | Two or more tracer concentrations; input function; Péclet number | Advective transport with superimposed hydrodynamic dispersion; described by a single Péclet parameter | More realistic than PFM for heterogeneous aquifers; single additional parameter beyond PFM | Péclet number poorly constrained without multi-tracer data; does not fully represent bimodal age distributions | Moderate; can be applied with 2–3 tracers; parameter uncertainty is high with sparse data | Turnadge & Smerdon (2014); Rädle et al. (2022) |
| Binary-mixing model | At least two tracers spanning different age windows; end-member compositions | Two discrete end-members (young \+ old) mix in variable proportions at a sampling point | Explicitly accounts for mixing of young recharge and old stored water; flexible | End-member ages and compositions must be specified; assumes only two mixing components | Moderate to good; captures old-water contamination vulnerability where 2-tracer data available | Casillas-Trasvina et al. (2022); Broers et al. (2021); Gil-Márquez et al. (2020) |
| Multi-component LPM / shape-free RTD | Three or more tracers spanning a wide age range; full atmospheric input functions | Multiple age fractions; RTD estimated by unconstrained or constrained inversion | Best representation of mixed-age groundwater; reduces non-uniqueness compared with single-tracer models | Requires large multi-tracer dataset; computationally intensive; still non-unique with few tracers | Poor in data-limited settings; applicable where dedicated multi-tracer campaigns are feasible | Rädle et al. (2022); McCallum et al. (2017) |
| Bayesian multi-tracer LPM | Two or more tracers; prior distributions on LPM parameters; atmospheric input history | Probabilistic model selection and parameter estimation; uncertainty in tracer measurement, input functions, and model type propagated explicitly | Provides probability distributions over RTD parameters; formally quantifies uncertainty; can compare models | Requires specification of priors; computationally demanding; interpretation requires statistical expertise | Limited by data requirements but conceptually ideal for propagating uncertainty under sparse data | Rädle et al. (2022); Thiros et al. (2023) |
| Numerical flow model \+ particle tracking (MODPATH) | Calibrated 3D groundwater-flow model (MODFLOW); hydraulic parameters; recharge and pumping records | Advective transport only; porosity uniform or specified; no mixing beyond numerical diffusion | Physically grounded; produces 3D RTDs; integrates hydrogeological complexity; can be compared against tracer ages | Requires extensive hydraulic data for model construction and calibration; not applicable without a numerical model | Poor in truly data-limited settings; applicable where public benchmark MODFLOW models exist or can be approximated | Starn et al. (2021); Baker et al. (2025); Meyer et al. (2018) |
| Metamodel / machine-learning approach | Landscape attributes, soil, geology, land use; training data from numerical simulation ensembles | Statistical relationships between observable landscape features and RTD metrics learned from simulation training sets | Fast prediction across large regions; can transfer to ungauged basins after training | Relies entirely on quality of training data; cannot extrapolate reliably beyond training domain | Potentially useful for regional screening; requires careful validation before application in African semi-arid settings | Starn et al. (2021); Starn & Belitz (2018) |

**Table 3\.** Graph-topology approaches in groundwater studies.

| Approach | Node definition | Edge definition | Directionality | Physical basis | Primary output | Key limitation | Key references |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Physical conduit network graph (karst / fractured rock) | Conduit intersections, sinkhole inlets, spring outlets, borehole collars | Individual conduit segments or fracture connections; hydraulic conductance or travel-time weights | Directed; flow direction from hydraulic gradient | Conduit geometry from speleological mapping, tracer tests, or geophysics | Conduit connectivity map; spring capture zones; solute transport pathways | Conduit geometry rarely fully observable; graph is a plausible realisation, not a unique solution | Malenica et al. (2018); Bodin et al. (2021); Gouy et al. (2024); Fandel et al. (2022) |
| Stochastic conduit-network graph (ensemble) | Recharge inlets, conduit intersections, spring outlets defined from geological constraints | Shortest-path or anisotropic fast-marching edges on an n-nearest-neighbour graph; cost function from stratigraphy, hydraulics, and speleogenesis | Directed; recharge-to-discharge | Geological and hydrological cost functions constrain edge feasibility | Ensemble of plausible conduit networks; probability of connection | Multiple equally plausible realisations; does not reproduce speleogenesis physics exactly | Fandel et al. (2022); Banusch et al. (2022); Gouy et al. (2024) |
| MODPATH particle-track graph (porous aquifer) | Model cells, well screens, recharge zones, surface-water reaches, ecological receptors | Directed edges from particle-crossing frequency maps; edge weights proportional to particle flux or travel-time distribution | Directed; defined by simulated hydraulic gradient and flow field | Grounded in calibrated numerical groundwater-flow model | Source-to-receptor connectivity map; travel-time distributions; edge-weighted directed graph priors | Depends entirely on quality of MODFLOW model; requires dense hydraulic data for calibration | Alberti et al. (2018); Gonzalez et al. (2020); Starn et al. (2021); Meyer et al. (2018) |
| Probabilistic preferential-flow network (porous aquifer) | Monitoring wells or model cells | Edges defined by probability that aquifer-bottom topographic gradient connects two nodes; steepest-descent or Monte Carlo sampling | Directed; steepest-gradient downslope logic | Aquifer-bottom elevation field; piezometric head gradients | Probabilistic preferential groundwater network; edge confidence from stochastic ensemble | Requires stratigraphic data for aquifer-bottom characterisation; does not encode fractures or conduits | Schiavo et al. (2022) |
| Sheaf-style consistency graph proposed as a transferable framework, not yet established as a groundwater-network method | Wells, springs, or model nodes with multi-variable hydrochemical, isotopic, and hydraulic observations | Edges from proposed hydraulic connectivity; restriction maps encode expected down-gradient changes in age, chemistry, and redox | Directed | Hydrogeological consistency rules (age increases, redox evolves, chemistry changes along expected path) | Global consistency score (consistency radius) per edge and per graph; identification of inconsistent subnetworks | Mathematically advanced; formal implementation in groundwater not yet demonstrated; requires multi-variable data at each node | Robinson (2020); Hansen & Ghrist (2019); Kvinge et al. (2021) |
| Statistical hydrochemical similarity graph | Sampling wells, springs, or hydrochemical clusters | Undirected edges from Pearson correlation, hydrochemical distance, PCA proximity, or HCA linkage among sample compositions | Undirected; reflects compositional similarity, not physical flow | Statistical similarity in major-ion, isotopic, or trace-element space | Hydrochemical communities; candidate hydrochemical families for inverse modelling | Does not represent physical flow; similar chemistry does not imply hydraulic connection; confusing with geographic graph | Tziritis et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2020); Roy et al. (2020) |
| Graph neural network (data-driven) | Groundwater-level monitoring sites or model cells | Learned edges from spatial correlations in groundwater-level time series; adjacency matrix optimised during training | Undirected or weakly directed; defined statistically | Statistical dependence in observed time series; no direct physical basis | Groundwater-level predictions across monitoring network | Learned edges do not correspond to physical flow paths or travel times; cannot be directly used for reaction or age modelling | Taccari et al. (2024); Bai & Tahmasebi (2023) |

**Table 4\.** Inverse hydrogeochemical modelling methods.

| Method | Reaction basis | Thermodynamic constraints | Flow-path requirement | Non-uniqueness handling | Output type | Data requirement | Key references |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| PHREEQC inverse modelling | User-specified candidate mineral phases, gas exchange, cation exchange, redox reactions between a defined initial and final water pair | Saturation index (SI) used to screen supersaturated vs. undersaturated phases; dissolving SI \< 0, precipitating SI \> 0 | User must nominate initial–final pair; no independent flow-path derivation | Multiple viable solutions reported; constrained by SI screening and user-specified mineral list; non-uniqueness not formally quantified | Mass-transfer values (mmol/L) per phase along one flow-path pair; speciation; SI map | Initial water chemistry; final water chemistry; candidate mineral phases; pCO2; redox indicators; well locations | Roy et al. (2020); Guo et al. (2025); Jagert et al. (2023); Rafiq et al. (2022) |
| NETPATH / NETPATH-WIN | Mass-balance reactions along a defined flow path; mineral phases, gas exchange, ion exchange, mixing with up to three end-members | Uses SI calculated by WATEQ4F as guidance; not a strict constraint in the fitting algorithm | Requires user-defined initial and final waters plus mixing end-members; flow path assumed not derived | Explores combinations of user-listed phases; reports all solutions satisfying mass-balance tolerances; uncertainty in mixing fraction quantified by isotope constraints | Net phase transfers (mmol/kg water); mixing fractions; isotope-balance check (δ13C, δ18O) | Initial and final water chemistry; δ13C if 14C-constrained; candidate mineral phases; mixing end-member compositions | Masoud et al. (2025); Srour et al. (2022); Akpataku et al. (2019); Gastmans et al. (2016) |
| Sparse inverse reaction fitting (combinatorial) | Minimum plausible set of reactions from systematically tested combinations of a constrained mineral pool derived from local geology | SI used as initial filter; only thermodynamically active phases included; mass-balance tolerances tightened | User selects sample pairs for comparison, typically grouped by PCA/HCA hydrochemical community | Systematic testing of all viable mineral assemblages; reports all solutions passing mass-balance \+ SI filter; reduces non-uniqueness by restricting phase list | Set of plausible minimal reaction assemblages per sample-group pair; ranked by number of phases and residual | Averaged or representative group chemistry; local mineralogy; δ13C / SI data; PCA/HCA grouping | Manu et al. (2023); Roy et al. (2020); Slimani et al. (2017) |
| Graph-constrained edge-based inverse modelling (proposed framework element, not an established modelling code) | Mass-balance reactions fitted along directed graph edges rather than arbitrary sample pairs; edge attributes (lithology, redox zone, residence-time window) constrain candidate phases | SI screening applied at each node and edge; reaction direction constrained by SI of initial node; reaction magnitude constrained by residence-time prior from isotope ages or particle tracking | Flow-path selection formally determined by directed confidence-weighted graph; only high-confidence edges used for inverse fitting | Multiple viable solutions per edge reported; cross-edge consistency checked; ensemble of graph realisations propagates topology uncertainty into reaction uncertainty | Network-scale geochemical process map; mass-transfer values per edge; consistency score per edge; probabilistic reaction-pathway inventory | Major ions at all nodes; SI at each node; directed graph with confidence weights; isotope-derived age at nodes; local mineralogy | Tziritis et al. (2023); Manu et al. (2023); Starn et al. (2021); Schiavo et al. (2022) |
| Forward reactive transport (PHREEQC / CrunchTope / FEFLOW) | Kinetic and equilibrium reactions coupled to transport; simulates chemical evolution spatially and temporally along a flow domain | Full thermodynamic equilibrium for fast reactions; kinetic rate laws for slow reactions; no assumption of initial–final pair required | Requires calibrated flow and transport model; flow path is an output, not an input | Uncertainty from kinetic rate constants, reactive surface areas, dispersivity, and model structure; non-uniqueness reduced by coupling to flow model but residual non-uniqueness in rate parameters | Spatially and temporally distributed concentrations of all species; reaction rates per grid cell; saturation state maps | Calibrated flow model; hydraulic parameters; dispersivity; mineralogy and reactive surface areas; temperature; redox boundary conditions | Rafiq et al. (2022); Blasco et al. (2019) |

Note: The graph-constrained edge-based inverse modelling row describes the framework proposed in this review. It is included to clarify how established inverse modelling tools could be reorganised around directed graph edges, but it should not be interpreted as an existing standalone modelling package equivalent to PHREEQC, NETPATH or forward reactive-transport codes.

**Table 6\.** Research gaps and methodological opportunities.

| Gap | Consequence if unaddressed | Required data | Suitable method | Expected contribution | Key references |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Age ambiguity in the intermediate range (\~100–10,000 yr) | Most data-limited aquifers in semi-arid Africa contain a mixture of Holocene and Pleistocene groundwater that cannot be distinguished by 3H/3He or 14C alone; sustainability assessments and vulnerability assessments are unreliable | Two or more complementary tracers: ideally 39Ar or 85Kr alongside 14C; δ13C; DIC; noble gases | Multi-tracer Bayesian LPM; ATTA for 39Ar and 81Kr; age-distribution modelling with explicit uncertainty propagation | Reduction in residence-time uncertainty; clearer separation of renewable from fossil storage; improved contamination vulnerability classification | Broers et al. (2021); Casillas-Trasvina et al. (2022); Rädle et al. (2022) |
| Subjective flow-path selection in inverse hydrogeochemical modelling | Non-unique and analyst-dependent reaction-pathway diagnoses; published reaction models cannot be independently reproduced or compared across studies | Piezometric head contours; well locations and screen depths; hydrochemical data at all nodes; basic geological map | Directed, confidence-weighted graph construction (Section 6.3); particle-track-based graph priors (Section 6.4); edge-constrained combinatorial inverse fitting (Section 6.5) | Reproducible, multi-evidence flow-path selection; reduction in number of viable reaction solutions; network-scale geochemical process maps instead of point-scale models | Tziritis et al. (2023); Manu et al. (2023); Schiavo et al. (2022) |
| Lack of formal uncertainty propagation across age, topology and reaction terms | Reported interpretations carry unquantified compounded uncertainty; management decisions based on single-scenario outputs may significantly misrepresent risk | Age uncertainty distributions from LPM or Bayesian analysis; graph-ensemble edge confidence scores; all viable inverse model solutions | Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation; stochastic graph ensembles; Bayesian updating; PHREEQC sensitivity analysis across viable phase lists | Probabilistic diagnostic outputs (vulnerability maps, source-apportionment estimates, reaction confidence maps) with explicit confidence bounds; outputs suited to risk-based management | Thiros et al. (2023); Gonzalez et al. (2020); Schiavo et al. (2023); Rädle et al. (2022) |
| Absence of open-source integrated workflow software | Methods remain isolated in separate disciplinary communities; integration is technically demanding and not accessible to agencies with limited modelling capacity | Standard PHREEQC input files; MODPATH output files; a well-documented graph construction and consistency-checking module | Open-source Python or R toolchain linking isotope LPM, MODPATH graph-prior generation, combinatorial inverse modelling, and uncertainty propagation | Lowered methodological barrier; standardised reporting templates; reproducibility of integrated studies; wider adoption in data-limited settings | Starn et al. (2021); Manu et al. (2023); Borzí (2025) |
| Non-uniqueness in 14C groundwater age correction in semi-arid, geochemically complex aquifers | 14C ages can differ by \>10,000 yr depending on correction model; false confidence in age estimates underpins incorrect sustainability or vulnerability assessments | Paired 14C–δ13C measurements; DIC; mineralogy; pCO2 and vadose-zone gas samples; multiple correction models applied to the same dataset | Statistical 14C–δ13C approach; full geochemical mass-balance model in PHREEQC; model comparison and explicit reporting of correction-model spread as part of age uncertainty | Quantified age uncertainty that honestly represents correction-model dependence; identification of cases where 14C age is unreliable without supporting data | Cartwright et al. (2019); Han & Plummer (2015); Seltzer et al. (2021) |
| Limited transferability of integrated frameworks from well-monitored to African semi-arid settings | Frameworks validated on dense North American or European datasets may fail in African basement, alluvial valley, or volcanic-rift aquifers with episodic recharge, thick vadose zones, and sparse data | Aquifer-type-specific minimum datasets; local GMWL/LMWL; tritium in precipitation; basic well construction metadata; major ions; δ2H and δ18O; at least one age indicator | Staged workflow (Section 6\) beginning with field EC/major ions/stable isotopes; adding 3H where feasible; constructing low-data graph from heads and geology; running constrained PHREEQC inverse models | Locally calibrated integrated frameworks for African aquifer types; minimum viable data specifications per workflow stage; demonstration case studies in pilot catchments | Borzí (2025); Cid-Escobar et al. (2023); Ferrer et al. (2019); Nowicki et al. (2023) |
| Disconnection between graph topology and physical hydrogeology (geometry vs. activity) | A topologically connected path may not be hydraulically active under current conditions; management actions based on geometric connectivity alone may be incorrect | Tracer tests or pump tests confirming hydraulic connectivity; piezometric head data; geophysical surveys; seasonal repeat sampling; redox and chemistry consistency checks | Sheaf-style consistency analysis across graph edges (Section 4.4); edge-confidence weighting using independent hydraulic, tracer, and chemical evidence; validation against independent geophysical data | Distinction between possible geometric connection and active hydraulic flow path; reduced false-positive connectivity; more reliable source-receptor and vulnerability assessments | Robinson (2020); Schiavo et al. (2022); Fandel et al. (2022); Bodin et al. (2021) |

**Note:** Suitability indicates potential use for workflow testing or benchmarking. It does not imply uniform availability of all tracer, hydrochemical, spatial and model variables across all sites, regions or records.
